Furthermore, the Government should prioritise mental health awareness and education 
campaigns to eliminate the stigma surrounding mental health issues by conducting awareness 
programs in schools and colleges, providing information on available mental health resources, 
and promoting open discussions on mental well-being. 
 
(Para 1.38 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.3.4 In some of the States, it has been found useful to increase awareness about helplines 
particularly before competitive examinations. Many newspapers are also carrying helpline 
numbers when they report any suicides and norms have also been developed for the media

Minister to address students’ academic stress before board examinations. Institutes like 
NIMHANS are working to bring out guidelines to manage such instances that are commonly 
seen in educational institutions (such as those in Kota, and Rajasthan). These guidelines will be

‘Manodarpan’, covering a wide range of activities to provide psychosocial support to students,

2.5 Analysis of Key Features of the Act 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.5.1 The Committee believes that the key challenge with implementing of advance directives 
is the need for more awareness and understanding among healthcare professionals and the 
general public. Individuals may need to be made aware of the provision or help understand how 
to create an advance directive effectively. Therefore, the Committee recommends the 
Government to put in adequate efforts to educate and raise awareness about advance directives 
to ensure their meaningful utilisation. Furthermore, the Committee believes that mental health 
conditions and circumstances may change over time, leading to alterations in an individual's 
preferences for treatment. The Act does not explicitly address the issue of periodic review and 
updating of advance directives. The Committee, therefore, recommends that regular review and 
the provision for modifying advance directives in response to evolving preferences and 
conditions should be considered to ensure their relevance and applicability. 
(Para 2.15 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.5.2 The public and key stakeholders require sensitization on all aspects of the Mental Health 
Care Act, including advance directives.  A recent program conducted by the NHRC with the 
participation of the Government has focused on issues related to both the implementation and 
awareness about the Mental Health Act. 
2.5.3 The concept of the Advance Directive and how it can be implemented in different 
contexts requires re-examination, in consultation with the respective stakeholders.

2.7 Insurance in Mental Healthcare 
Recommendations/Observations:  
 
2.7.1 The Committee notes the provision in the Mental Healthcare Act for medical insurance 
for treating mental illness on the same lines as is available for treating physical illness. The

Committee, however, recommends the Ministry to work in tandem with IRDAI and encourage the 
insurance providers to include more and more mental health issues in the insurance policies as 
the Committee feels that insurance policies traditionally are designed to cater to the in-patient 
procedures. Thus insurance providers might not be willing to include mental health procedures 
primarily out-patient, viz. counselling sessions. 
(Para 2.25 of the Report) 
Action Taken:

recommendations regarding insurance related to mental illness. The same will be examined by 
the Ministry for further action. 
 
Recommendations/Observations:

the insurance delivery for mental health issues; the Government should ascertain data on 
policies covering mental health issues, total claims received for mental issues, total claims 
cleared, rejection of policies and reasons for rejection. The Committee further recommends the 
Ministry to actively pursue IRDAI to discourage the insurance providers from excluding 

18 
 
treatment for attempted suicide or self-injury as both of these may require treatment or 
hospitalisation. 
(Para 2.26 of the Report) 
Action Taken:

Recommendations/Observations:

(Para 2.30 of the Report)

2.9 Mental Health Program and Mental Health Infrastructure 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
2.9.1 The committee acknowledges the measures taken under NMHP and DMHP to integrate 
mental health services with Primary and Secondary health services. The Committee believes 
that quality mental health services if provided at the Primary and Secondary levels, will result 
in fewer cases requiring treatment at the tertiary level. Also, the capital expenditure for 
augmenting the primary and secondary mental health facilities is far lower than the budgetary 
requirements for developing tertiary mental healthcare infrastructure. Also, the expenditure 
(public and out-of-pocket) for treating mental illnesses is comparatively lower if mental issues 
can be screened early at the PHC and CHC levels (as shown in the pyramid below under 3.12). 
Therefore, the Committee recommends the Ministry to take appropriate measures and allocate 
sufficient funds to strengthen primary and secondary mental health services. For this, the 
Ministry should develop improved monitoring systems to oversee the functioning of the DMHP 
and to generate reliable data on the functioning of the DMHP.  The data generated can be used 
to update/ upgrade the DMHP for better functioning. 
 (Para 3.10 of the Report) 

19 
 
Action Taken: 
2.9.2 To strengthen mental health service delivery at the primary care level, mental health care 
is now included as one of the components of the ‘Comprehensive Primary Mental Healthcare’ 
Packages of the Ayushman Bharat. Mental health is one of the 12 packages.  
2.9.3 The guidelines to manage mental, neurological, and substance use disorders at the Health 
and Wellness Centres are made available for States and UTs.  
2.9.4 The functioning of DMHP and footfall is also monitored as a part of the Output Outcome 
Monitoring Framework (OOMF) of NITI Aayog, besides internal monitoring through review 
mechanisms in the Ministry such as during National Programme Co-ordinating Committees 
(NPCC) Meetings held with States/UTs and Common Review Missions (CRM) of National 
Health Mission. 
Recommendations/Observations: 
2.9.5 Furthermore, the Committee believes that at the primary level i.e. at in DMHP, along 
with the existing biomedical approach, equal focus, if not more, should be given to community-
based care. The Committee believes that community-based care offers a person-centered and 
community-oriented approach to mental health, promoting accessibility, early intervention, 
holistic care, integration, reduced stigma, and continuity of support. It recognises the 
importance of addressing mental health within the broader social fabric and promoting well-
being at the community level. Therefore, the Committee recommends that under DMHP, the 
Ministry devise treatment/ rehabilitation/ counselling measures rooted in community-based care. 
The DMHP should work beyond the clinical services and also focus on awareness of mental 
health issues, mitigate stigma through its outreach activities, improve intersectoral action and 
build linkages with other health initiatives, viz. TB elimination programme to strengthen overall 
well-being. 
(Para 3.11 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.9.6 The Ministry has developed guidelines for treating mental health issues for non-
specialists including medical officers, psychologists, social workers, and nurses. 
 
2.9.7 Institutes such as NIMHANS, have come up with simpler tools for (a) doctors (Clinical 
Schedules of Primary Care Psychiatry) and (b) Community Health Workers (the MERIT 
screening tool for screening commonly prevalent mental health issues in communities). These 
are already being used in States such as Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Uttarakhand, etc. Efforts will 
be made to ensure these measures reach the country. Efforts are also on to link up other national 
programs (viz the Leprosy Eradication Program and the TB elimination Program) with mental 
health aspects.

Recommendations/Observations:  
 
2.10.1 The Committee notes that the average of 0.75 mental health professionals for every 
100,000 people is meagre and the lack of numbers is reflected on the ground where millions of 

20 
 
people battling the range of mental health issues continue to suffer – not only because of stigma 
and ignorance but also because there are insufficiently trained mental health professionals. The 
Committee feels that if even the target is three Psychiatrists (per 100,000 population) as the 
desired number, India needs 36,000 psychiatrists to reach that goal. So, currently, India is short 
of 27,000 psychiatrists. Not considering attrition and other factors, at the rate of 1000 new 
psychiatrists, it may take India another 27 years to achieve the target. The scenario is more or 
less the same for other mental health professionals viz. psychologists, psychiatric social workers 
and nurses. 
(Para 3.20 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.10.2 Under the tertiary care component of NMHP, 25 Centres of Excellence have been 
sanctioned to increase the intake of students in PG departments in mental health specialties as 
well as to provide tertiary-level treatment facilities.  Further, the Government has also 
supported 19 Government medical colleges/institutions to strengthen 47 PG Departments in 
mental health specialties. Mental Health Services are also provisioned for 22 AIIMS. These 
services are also available under PMJAY. 
 
2.11 Manpower Development 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.11.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry not to terminate the Manpower 
Development Scheme in 2024 and continue it beyond, as it is vital to augment the availability of 
mental health professionals to achieve the set target within a decade. The Committee 
recommends the NMC (National Medical Commission) through the Ministry to actively explore 
the feasibility of augmenting the MD Psychiatry seats in the medical colleges. The Committee 
also suggests the Ministry to examine the possibility of 3 year DNB degree in Psychiatry and 
other mental health specialisation in private hospitals, Railway hospitals, PSU hospitals etc, 
through the National Board of Examinations. 
(Para 3.21 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.11.2 The proposal for the continuation of the Manpower Development Scheme under NMHP 
beyond 2024 is under consideration in the Ministry. The feasibility will be examined in the 
Ministry in consultation with other stakeholders. 
 
2.12 Discontinuance of M.Phil. Courses 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
2.12.1 The Committee further recommends the Ministry to expedite the solution of the problem 
which has emanated due to the discontinuation of the M. Phil courses as per the New Education 
Policy. The Committee believes that Clinical Psychologist is an essential mental health resource 
and thus suggests that the Ministry may explore re-naming the course or any other alternative 
and thus relieve the candidates who have already joined for the course. 
(Para 3.22 of the Report) 

21 
 
 
Action Taken: 
 
2.12.2 This has been examined by the Niti Aayog and the Ministry has constituted a committee 
of all stakeholders in this regard. A recommendation has been proposed in line with the NEP. 
 
2.13 Nimhans (National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences) 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.13.1 To further enhance its impact and fulfil its visionary goals, the Committee recommends 
NIMHANS to focus on expanding outreach programs to underserved communities, fostering 
collaborative research initiatives with national and international institutions, and advocating 
for mental health awareness at the national level. The Committee believes that strengthening the 
training programs for mental health professionals and embracing technological advancements 
in the field will also be instrumental in advancing patient care and research capabilities. 
(Para 3.29 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
2.13.2 NIMHANS is constantly taking up new outreach programs in collaboration with State 
Governments, international agencies and NGOs. For research in mental health, one example is 
the establishment of the Centre for Brain and Mind with support from RNK foundation. Another 
is collaboration for dual-PHDs with the University of Liverpool and Maastricht. Nurses from the 
University of Oslo are receiving training at NIMHANS. 
2.13.3 In the area of psycho-social interventions for disaster mitigation, NIMHANS is providing 
the psycho-social care component for the National Disaster Management Authority. Training is 
also being provided to countries like Fiji. 
2.13.4 Human resource capacity building for primary care has been facilitated for Bangladesh 
and Bhutan. Psychiatrists from Nepal have been provided training in child psychiatry. 
 
2.14 NIMHANS Digital Academy (NDA) 
 
Recommendations/Observations:  
 
2.14.1 The Committee strongly recommends the Government to take significant steps towards 
expanding the NIMHANS Digital Academy (NDA) nationwide, as it presents a remarkable 
opportunity to revolutionise mental health education and training nationwide.  By leveraging 
the digital platform, NDA can bridge the gap in mental health services and ensure that quality 
training is accessible to mental health professionals in Primary Health Centers (PHCs), 
Community Health Centers (CHCs), and district hospitals. To achieve this, the Government 
should allocate adequate resources to scale up NDA's infrastructure and content creation, 
ensuring seamless access to courses for mental health professionals in remote and rural areas. 
Additionally, mental health professionals should be given incentives and encouragement to take 

22 
 
courses through NDA, much like Government officials participate in capacity-building courses 
under the Karmyogi Bharat program. 
(Para 3.32 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.14.2 A proposal to expand the activities of the NIMHANS Digital Academy has been 
submitted to the Ministry and is under examination. Under the expanded NDA there is scope to 
train at least 6500 each of doctors, psychologists, nurses and 10,000 other individuals annually.  
There is scope to convert the NDA into a Digital University to increase human resources for all 
aspects of mental health care in the country. 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.14.3 The Committee further recommends the Government to collaborate with state 
Governments, medical institutions, and NGOs to enhance the reach and impact of NDA further. 
This partnership will enable a wider dissemination of knowledge and expertise, empowering 
mental health professionals with evidence-based practices and the latest advancements in the 
field. Furthermore, the Government should focus on the localisation of content to cater to 
diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds, making the courses more inclusive and relevant for 
mental health professionals working in different regions of the country. By fostering a culture of 
continuous learning and professional development through NDA, mental health professionals in 
PHCs, CHCs, and district hospitals will be equipped with the necessary skills and knowledge to 
address the growing mental health needs of the population effectively. 
(Para 3.33 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
2.14.4 NDA’s aim is to collaborate with State Governments, medical institutions and NGOs to 
enhance the reach and to enable a wider dissemination of knowledge and expertise. 
2.14.5 Many state Govts are working in collaboration with NDA including Karnataka, 
Maharashtra, Jammu and Kashmir, Gujarat, Odisha, Bihar, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Haryana, 
Arunachal Pradesh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, etc. 
2.14.6 Through NDA, mental health professionals in PHCs, CHCs, and district hospitals are 
being equipped with the necessary skills and knowledge to address the growing mental health 
needs of the population effectively. 
 
2.15 Hub and Spoke Model for Mental Health 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.15.1 The Committee takes note of the "Hub and Spoke Model" suggested by NIMHANS and 
understands its importance in strengthening mental healthcare services in all regions of the 
country. The Committee recommends the Government to adopt and expand the Hub and Spoke 
model for mental health care across the entire country, following the successful implementation 
of a similar model employed in cancer care by Tata Memorial Hospital. This approach can 

23 
 
potentially revolutionise mental health infrastructure and expertise, particularly in peripheral 
centres, and ensure better accessibility and quality of care.  
(Para 3.40 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.15.2 NIMHANS, in collaboration with the ECHO program has already initiated a hub and 
spoke model, initially for substance use and subsequently for various areas in mental health. 
NIMHANS is committed to delivering this through the NDA. 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
2.15.3 These hubs at prominent institutions with specialised expertise, resources, and state-of-
the-art facilities can serve as centres of excellence, offering mental health professionals 
comprehensive diagnostic, treatment, and training services. In North India, IHBAS, New Delhi 
can be brought under Central Government and set up as a hub; similarly, LGBRIMH, Tezpur 
can be set up as a hub for East India, CIP, Ranchi for Central India and NIMHANS, Bengaluru 
South India. Furthermore, the Government should develop a network of spoke centres in rural 
and remote areas strategically connected to the hubs. These centres would act as primary care 
providers and offer essential mental health services while being supported and guided by the 
expertise available at the hubs. The Committee also recommends the Government to grant the 
status of “Institute of National Importance” to LGBRIMH, Tezpur and CIP, Ranchi. 
 (Para 3.41 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.15.4 Yes, as mentioned in this recommendation, IHBAS, CIP and LGB are functioning as the 
Regional Coordinating Centres (RCCs) for Tele MANAS and are assisting the Govt in the 
implementation of Tele MANAS. The same model will be adopted for overall mental healthcare 
and training as well, across the country. The Karnataka Brain Health Initiative seeks to train 
primary and secondary healthcare professionals in the identification, management, and referral of 
common neurological disorders. It is subsequently expected that a common framework of 
managing Mental, Neurological, and substance use disorders would be developed in consonance 
with WHO recommendations. To create a comprehensive care model, it is envisaged to develop 
a hub and spoke for acute stroke and head injuries and such a proposal has been made to the 
Govt of Karnataka, to develop 6 spokes for acute stroke and neurotrauma care with NIMHANS 
as the hub. This will work complementarily with the Karnataka Brain Health Initiative, which 
has been presently approved for rollout in all districts. 
 
2.16 Budgetary Allocation for Telemanas (T-Manas) Scheme 
Recommendations/Observations:  
 
2.16.1 The Committee further believes that while T-MANAS is a valuable initiative, it cannot be 
viewed as a comprehensive solution for long-term mental health improvement, nor should it be 
the sole focus of the Government's efforts. Instead, investing in and enhancing community-based 
mental healthcare services is essential. Strengthening the District Mental Health Programme 

24 
 
(DMHP) at the community level, as directed by the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, and developing 
other community-based models of mental health is of utmost importance and should continue to 
receive appropriate budgetary allocations. T-MANAS can complement community-based 
approaches and help establish a more comprehensive and sustainable mental health support 
system for the people of the country. 
(Para 3.51 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
2.16.2 Tele MANAS is functioning as the digital arm of the National Mental Health Program, 
and its objective is exactly as is mentioned in the recommendation: to compliment the 
community-based approaches and referral system to higher institutions and help establish a more 
comprehensive and sustainable mental health support system for the people of the country. 
2.16.3 As regards developing community-based models, already piloting of the Taluk Mental 
Health Program has started in Karnataka. NIMHANS has also started NAMAN (NIMHANS-
Ashraya Hasta Trust Mental Health Action Program for Rural Communities), the objective of 
which is the implementation and evaluation of a comprehensive and holistic mental health 
program in rural talukas in vastly different geographies of the country. The results of NAMAN 
will help us expand the initiative across the country. 
  

25 
 
CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
3.1 Mental Health Issues in Children and Youth 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
3.1.1 The Committee notes the findings of "World Mental Health Report- Transforming 
Mental Health for All" and believes that childhood experiences significantly affect behavioural 
aspects. The Committee understands that behavioural aspects play a crucial role in mental 
health as they can significantly influence an individual's well-being, coping mechanisms, and 
overall mental state. The Committee, therefore, urges the Government to adopt a multi-faceted 
approach that involves collaboration between the Government, healthcare providers, 
educational institutions, and the community to address the behavioural aspects of mental 
health. The Government can invest in public awareness campaigns to educate citizens about the 
importance of mental health and the role of behavioural aspects. These campaigns can promote 
healthy habits, coping skills, and ways to seek help when needed. The Committee further 
suggests that the Government work with employers to implement workplace wellness programs 
focusing on mental health. These initiatives can include stress management workshops, 
counselling services, and flexible work arrangements to reduce stress. Similarly, the 
implementation of mental health education in schools can teach young individuals about 
behavioural aspects that contribute to mental well-being. This can equip them with the tools 
they need to manage their emotions and cope with challenges effectively. The Government 
should also invest in research to better understand the behavioural aspects that impact mental 
health and the effectiveness of different interventions. 
(Para 1.28 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
3.1.2 School mental health is made part of the National Mental Health Program as one of the 
targeted interventions. Collaboration with the Education Ministry at the centre and the state level 
is imperative to achieve this objective. Teaching life skills to children and adolescents are one of 
the most important aspects of these initiatives. A separate budget of 4 lakhs per district per 
annum is earmarked for IEC activities under the DMHP.In addition, the mental health is now 
being made part of the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram and the Rashtriya Kishore Swasthya 
Karyakram. The Ayushman Bharat revised School Health Program includes a component of 
child mental health. Recognizing the importance of workplace mental health, States/UTs will be 
encouraged to include workplace interventions as part of NMHP/DMHP.As regards research, the 
Indian Council of Medical Research and other funding agencies are dedicating funds for 
effectiveness and implementation research in mental health. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.1.3 The Committee notes that despite its nearly decade-long existence the 
implementation of Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) launched in 2014 to 
focus solely on addressing adolescent health concerns has progressed at a very slow pace. 
The Committee notes that RKSK has not disclosed data concerning crucial components 

26 
 
such as mental health, violence, injuries, and substance misuse. Similarly, other initiatives, 
such as the Sarva Shiksha Yojana (focused on learning disabilities), the National Youth 
Policy (addressing substance abuse), the National Mental Health Policy, and the Yuva 
Spandana Yojana (implemented only in Karnataka) targeting adolescents have failed to 
treat mental health as a primary issue. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to make concerted efforts in spreading the awareness of RKSK among school-
going adolescents, parents, and teachers in both the rural and the urban areas, as well as 
in slums of urban centres like Mumbai. The Ministry should also work towards promoting 
and popularising its digital interventions like mobile app called ‘Saathiya Salah’.  
 
3.2 Increased Awareness of Trained Human Resource: 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
3.2.1 Furthermore, the Committee believes there is still scope for policy and programmatic 
interventions to effectively prioritise and address the underlying factors, viz., vulnerable groups, 
unemployed youth, women, and others contributing to mental health issues. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to integrate psycho- social interventions targeted at specific 
vulnerable groups into schemes and programs, such as those related to social justice, women's 
empowerment, and child development. The Committee further recommends enhancing inter 
sectoral collaborations and establishing synergy among different ministries, departments, and 
agencies while implementing NMHP. 
(Para 2.10 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
3.2.2 The Ministry will initiate steps to integrate mental health into policies and programmatic 
interventions of other sectors. 
 One such example is the SAMVAD that is led by the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development and is in force since the past couple of years. SAMVAD, a unique national 
initiative and integrated resource for child protection, mental health and psycho-social 
care named ‘Support Advocacy and Mental health interventions for children in 
Vulnerable Circumstances and Distress’ (SAMVAD) has developed standardized training 
modules for capacity building of all key stakeholders working in the area of child and 
adolescent mental health in child protection, policy and laws. More than 3 million 
stakeholders across the country have been reached through SAMVAD.  
 Several life skills programmes have been initiated to empower adolescents.  
 Mission Vatsalya from the WCD which focuses on children in difficult circumstances has 
issued guidelines for implementation of psychosocial support for children as per Juvenile 
Justice Care and Protect Act 2015. 
 To ensure women’s mental health, one-stop centres have been initiated by the WCD. 
These programmes have scope for expansion.  
 
Further Recommendation: 
 
3.2.3 The Committee further recommends that to integrate mental health into policies 
the policymakers should endeavour to strive towards transitioning from the prevailing 

27 
 
"medical model" of mental health to the convergent model. This approach acknowledges 
the intricate interaction among behavioural, environmental, biological, and genetic 
elements across an individual's lifespan, particularly during pivotal stages like childhood 
and adolescence. In pursuit of this objective, initiatives such as RKSK can learn from the 
practices of other nations like United States where the successful implementation of the 
‘Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child’ model embraces a holistic approach to 
children’s well-being by considering factors such as nutrition, physical activity, and 
emotional health within the school environment. The Committee further believes that 
initiatives like establishing peer support groups in schools and colleges and community-
based interventions leveraging technology can also encourage help-seeking behaviour. 
 
3.3 Analysis of Key Features of the Act 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
3.3.1 The Committee further recommends the Ministry to conduct periodic training programs 
through CMHA and SMHAs for police personnel, people associated with the judiciary and also 
general health practitioners to sensitise them about their responsibilities and about the different 
provisions and issues concerning mental health of the MHCA.  
(Para 2.23 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
3.3.2 In some states, training initiatives are being undertaken by the Judicial Academies and 
psychiatry departments in medical colleges. 
 
Further Recommendation: 
 
3.3.3 The Committee further recommends the Ministry to take more concrete measures 
to address the training needs for various stakeholders concerning mental health provisions. 
The Committee suggests the Ministry to establish a nationwide mandatory training 
program specifically designed for police personnel, judiciary members, and general health 
practitioners. This program should be comprehensive, ensuring that participants are 
sensitized to their responsibilities under the Mental Health Care Act (MHCA) and 
equipped with the necessary knowledge and skills to effectively address mental health 
issues in their respective roles. Additionally, the Ministry should allocate adequate 
resources to facilitate the implementation of these training programs, ensuring their 
accessibility and effectiveness across all states and regions. 
 
3.4 Budgetary Allocation to Premier Mental Health Institutions 
 
Recommendations/Observations: 
 
3.4.1 The Committee notes that NIMHANS is India's premier mental health and neurosciences 
research institute. However, compared to NIMH in the United States, NIMHANS receives 
relatively limited funding from the Indian Government. While the Indian Government does 
allocate funds to NIMHANS, it might not be sufficient to meet the growing demand for mental 

28 
 
health services in the country. The Committee further notes that substantial funding allows 
NIMH to conduct cutting-edge research on mental health disorders, develop innovative 
treatments, and support various research projects nationwide. Additionally, NIMH collaborates 
with numerous academic and medical institutions, fostering a robust mental health research 
ecosystem. On the other hand, NIMHANS, despite having an excellent reputation and expertise, 
faces challenges due to limited resources. While it strives to provide quality mental health 
services and research, the constraints on funding can hinder its ability to reach a broader 
population and invest in advanced research endeavours. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Government to significantly increase budgetary allocations to mental health institutions like 
NIMHANS and LGBRIMH, Tezpur, as adequate funding is crucial for research, infrastructure 
development, and expanding mental health services to underserved areas. 
 (Para 3.48 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
3.4.2 Expanding quality care and comprehensive care at affordable or subsidized costs to 
patients is critical. In this connection, NIMHANS has submitted two proposals, one for a new 
outpatient block to substitute its outdated outpatient facility that was built in the mid- 1980s and 
a state of art polytrauma facility in its northern campus in Kyalasanahalli. 
3.4.3 For improved mental health and neuroscience care service delivery, human resources are 
a critical component. Under the 12th 5 year plan, NIMHANS had put in a proposal for 1680 
posts. Of this some posts were sanctioned but there were 1380 pending posts. In discussion with 
the Ministry, in 2020, this was first reduced to 780, then reduced to 457. Of these the DOE has 
only sanctioned 106 posts. The remaining posts as well as posts requested from the 7to 10GB 
still remain to be sanctioned. 
3.4.4 The Budgetary allocation of NIMHANS is Rs. 721.15 crores, as per BE 2023-24. 
However, inadvertently, the amount of 1500 and 2000 crores is shown in Figure 9 under point 
3.48 F on page 34 of the Report. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.4.5 The Committee believes that from the action taken by the Ministry it is evident that 
there remains a significant gap in addressing the funding and resource challenges faced by 
premier mental health institutions like NIMHANS. Therefore, the Committee further 
recommends the following measures to be taken: 
1. Urgent allocation of adequate funding: The Government should prioritise and 
substantially increase budgetary allocations to mental health institutions such as 
NIMHANS and LGBRIMH, Tezpur. Adequate funding is crucial not only for 
sustaining existing services but also for enhancing infrastructure, research 
capabilities, and expanding mental health services to underserved areas. 
2. Expedite Human Resource Sanctions: Addressing the pending posts and expediting 
the sanctioning process for requested positions is paramount. Human resources are 
a critical component in delivering quality mental health care, and the delay in 
sanctioning posts hampers the institution's ability to meet the growing demand for 
services. 

29 
 
3. Clarification and Transparency in Budgetary Reporting: The Government should 
ensure accuracy and transparency in reporting budgetary allocations for mental 
health institutions. Inadvertent discrepancies, such as those noted in the reported 
figures, should be rectified promptly to provide clarity and facilitate effective 
resource planning. 
4. Long-term Strategic Planning: Develop a comprehensive long-term strategic plan 
for mental health care, research, and infrastructure development. This plan should 
outline clear goals, timelines, and resource allocation strategies to address the 
evolving needs of the mental health sector and ensure sustainable growth and 
excellence in service delivery. 
  

30

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1 Healthcare Access and Affordability in India 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee is of the view that health insurance is a mechanism of pooling the high 
level of OOPE in India to provide greater financial protection against health shocks and improve 
efficiency in the organization and delivery of healthcare for better health outcomes. Increased 
health insurance coverage will reduce catastrophic and impoverishing health expenditures by 
imposing a ceiling on the maximum health expenditure incurred by an individual or household. 
The publicly funded health insurance schemes are envisaged as keystone to advance Universal 
Health Coverage. 
(Para 1.2.7 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 AB PM-JAY has efficiently delivered the healthcare services to the target population 
resulting in huge OOPE saving for the beneficiaries. It has strengthened India’s march towards 
Universal Health Coverage. 
1.1.3 The beneficiary base under AB PM-JAY has been increasing over the years. Initially, 
when the scheme was launched, 10.74 crore beneficiary families under AB PM-JAY were 
targeted which was increased to 12 crore families in January 2022. Further, over the years of 
scheme implementation, various other vulnerable groups identified by the Government like 
PVTG, ASHAs (ASHAs) / Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) / Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) have 
been included under the scheme. 
1.1.4 Further, it may kindly be noted that one of the core principles around which AB PM-JAY 
has been designed is to ensure appropriate convergence with the existing health 
insurance/protection schemes of various Central Ministries/Departments and State Governments. 
This ensures comprehensive coverage for catastrophic illness, establish national standards for 
health assurance systems and provide national portability of care. As on date, 24 States/UTs have 
converged their State schemes with AB PM-JAY. Further, central government schemes like those 
for transgenders and manual scavengers have also been converged with AB PM-JAY. Also, NHA 
has onboarded multiple schemes on its platform which include CGHS, Ayushman CAPF, ESIC, 
BoCW, RAN-HMDG, PM-CARES. Efforts are being made for convergence with more schemes.  
 
1.2 Coverage of beneficiaries under PMJAY 

2 
 
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee believes that the Ministry and NHA, along with implementing States/UTs, 
need to undertake a country-wide drive to scrutinise and validate the BIS database. Validation 
checks should be in place to increase the accuracy and reliability of the data. The inconsistencies 
in the database may be removed at the earliest. The appropriate mechanism may be devised to 
ensure weeding out of ineligible beneficiaries and identification of eligible beneficiaries in a 
planned, coordinated and time-bound manner. States/UTs need to be impressed upon to map 
their own database with the SECC database to avoid duplication. The process for approval or 
rejection of ineligible beneficiaries and registration of eligible beneficiaries needs to be made 
simple and less time-consuming to avoid delay beyond the prescribed time. 
(Para 2.3.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 Initially when the scheme was started, it intended to cover 10.74 crore families identified 
from the Socio-economic Caste Census (SECC) of 2011. Further, the Cabinet of Government of 
India, in 2022, approved a revision in beneficiary base under AB PM-JAY from 10.74 crore to 12 
crore families considering India’s decadal population growth of 11.7 % over 2011 population. 
Many States and UTs have further expanded the beneficiary base with 13 States/UTs adopting 
Universal Health Coverage. To ensure that eligible beneficiaries get covered under the scheme, 
States/UTs have been provided the flexibility to choose other non-SECC beneficiary database 
which matches the profile of the beneficiary with that of AB PM-JAY.  
1.2.3 Further, to ensure that eligible beneficiaries are identified and issued Ayushman card with 
certainty, NHA has adopted a 3-pronged strategy which is as follows: 
i. National Health Authority has issued guidelines to States/UTs to use suitable Aadhaar 
seeded digitized databases of beneficiaries of similar socio-economic profile as that of 
eligible SECC beneficiaries. 
ii. Aadhaar based de-duplication of the beneficiary databases have been undertaken at the time 
of ingestion. 
iii. Aadhaar based e-KYC has been mandated for all beneficiaries. 
1.2.4 The States have also been asked to ensure that their databases are updated to weed out any 
ineligible beneficiary. It is important to note that when these databases are ingested in the BIS, 
Aadhaar based mapping is undertaken to ensure data de-duplication. 
1.2.5 Along with this, it is pertinent to note that the beneficiary verification process has been 
simplified with the launch of new ‘Ayushman app’ with self-verification process where an 
individual can create an Ayushman card for himself/herself. Also, the new system is equipped 
with the latest technology like face-auth which mitigates the need for any external device at the 
time of bio-authentication. 

3 
 
Recommendation 
1.2.6 The Committee recommends that the NHA needs to develop an IT-based solution to 
educate and create awareness that a family is eligible for the scheme, and ways to rapidly 
identify the family if any member comes to an empanelled hospital for treatment. 
(Para 2.3.9 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.7 Under AB PM-JAY, various measures have been undertaken to raise awareness about the 
scheme among eligible beneficiaries. 
1.2.8 In this regard, it may kindly be noted that the beneficiary verification process has been 
simplified with the launch of new ‘Ayushman app’ which has a self-verification process, wherein 
any individual can create an Ayushman card for himself/herself. Also, the new system is 
equipped with the latest technology like face-auth which mitigates the need for any external 
device at the time of bio-authentication.  
1.2.9 In the current IT system (BIS 2.0), the beneficiary search has been enabled using 
Aadhaar, Family ID such as ration card, Name along with location/address. Further, the line 
listing of beneficiaries has been provided in the BIS along with the Status of beneficiary 
identification. 
Recommendation 
1.2.10 The Committee believes that the Information, Education and Communication (IEC) 
programs are significant to understanding the various target audiences for PMJAY, like their 
attitudes and perceptions towards the scheme, and to educate the target audience about the 
scheme driving changes in their attitudes and behaviour. The programs are necessary to 
maximise the reach, impact, and awareness of the scheme amongst targeted beneficiaries. NHA 
needs to set up designated IEC cells, make special efforts in a planned manner and sensitise the 
entitled beneficiaries to generate awareness about the scheme. NHA should coordinate with 
SHAs and NGOs to design a comprehensive IEC plan and undertake IEC campaigns in a 
planned manner. Such IEC efforts should be recorded, reviewed, and monitored regularly. 
(Para 2.3.10 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.11 Under AB PM-JAY, a separate IEC division is operational at NHA level for planning and 
executing all IEC related requirement of the scheme. Further, all States have been advised to 
setup separate IEC cell to undertake various IEC campaigns to increase beneficiary awareness 
about the scheme.  

4 
 
1.2.12 Under AB PM-JAY, a comprehensive media and outreach strategy to spread awareness 
and empowering the beneficiaries about their entitlements and rights under the scheme has been 
followed. This included the use of media vehicles such as outdoor media, digital display 
announcements at major bus stations, national and regional press coverage, op-eds and 
advertorials in print media, radio campaign, telecast of beneficiary testimonials via Doordarshan, 
mass messaging. Further, NHA collaborated with Indian Railways for beneficiary awareness 
through public announcements at various railway stations. Also, train wrapping with scheme 
related information has been undertaken to spread awareness among beneficiaries.  
1.2.13 Further, a comprehensive media plan prepared by experts has been implemented during 
FY 2023-24. Also, NHA has issued a detailed IEC guideline which is available on the website 
(https://pmjay.gov.in/resources/iec).  
1.3 Coverage of beneficiaries under PMJAY 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee notes that the flexibility has been given to the States/UTs to choose the 
remaining beneficiaries from any digital database that the State/UT has if the broad nature of 
these new people matches with the beneficiary nature of PMJAY. The Committee is of the view 
that under that dispensation, States/UTs may be asked to include senior citizens, particularly 
those residing in old age homes or any other place by revising the Deprivation Criteria, as 
beneficiaries of the scheme. Many senior citizens residing in places like shelter homes and old 
age homes do not fall under the Below Poverty Line and face financial problems while availing 
treatments. Their inclusion in the scheme would help them access affordable and quality 
treatment. 
(Para 2.3.11 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 Initially, 10.74 crore beneficiary families under AB PM-JAY were targeted based on the 
Socio-economic Caste Census (SECC) of 2011 using select deprivation and occupational criteria 
across rural and urban areas respectively to identify the families. Further, in January 2022, the 
Cabinet of the Government of India, revised the beneficiary base to 12 crore families and decided 
to give flexibility to use other digitized databases of similar socio-economic profile for 
identification of beneficiaries under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. Accordingly, States/UTs have 
been given flexibility to use suitable databases for beneficiary identification. This is aimed to 
ensure that all eligible beneficiaries are provided free healthcare. In addition, many States/UTs 
implementing AB PM-JAY have expanded the beneficiary base under the scheme, at their own 
cost. 
1.3.3 Further, since all members of an eligible family are entitled for healthcare coverage under 
AB PM-JAY, senior citizens in such eligible families are also covered under the scheme. 

5 
 
1.3.4 The suggestion regarding inclusion of old aged persons as a separate category has been 
noted.  
1.4 Implementation Process- PMJAY 
Recommendation 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that there is a trend amongst the States to prefer the trust model 
and is of the view that the States opt for this model owing to their experience of working with the 
insurance companies. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to explore 
provisions to modify and improve the modalities related to the insurance mode to make it 
simpler, transparent, and attractive to the States. This will provide more options for the States to 
implement the scheme according to their regional demography and needs. The outgo of funds is 
immediate in insurance mode. The Committee suggests that the Government should push for 
payment of premium of insurance in instalments, preferably monthly/quarterly instalments.  
(Para 2.4.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.4.2 Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY is being implemented in 33 States and Union Territories 
(UTs). Various States / UTs are at different levels of preparedness and have varying capacity to 
manage the scheme. Accordingly, under PM-JAY they have been provided with the flexibility to 
implement the scheme through trust, insurance or mixed model (combination of trust and 
insurance). 
1.4.3 Further, NHA shares the feedback on the performance of the scheme with the States 
highlighting deficiencies, if any, on the part of insurance companies.   
1.4.4 In this regard, it may kindly be noted that at the time of launch of the scheme, many 
States/UTs did not have experience of implementing cashless health assurance scheme, therefore, 
SHAs opted for insurance or mixed mode of implementation. However, as the scheme progressed 
and the States/UTs gained experience of running the scheme and therefore, migrated to trust 
mode of implementation.   
1.4.5 Regarding, payment of premium in instalments, it may be noted that States have defined 
different payment terms to insurance companies. Accordingly, few States release premium on a 
quarterly basis, others in three instalments of 45:45:10 etc.  
Recommendation 
1.4.6 The Committee further believes that the Government should evaluate the performance of 
insurance companies. The Government should explore a robust monitoring mechanism to keep a 
check on any unjustified profit-making and any unethical linkage between the insurance 
companies and hospitals. Necessary mechanisms should be in place to ensure that the insurance 
companies are working as per the objectives and norms of the scheme. 

6 
 
(Para 2.4.5 of the Report) 
Action Taken  
1.4.7 The performance of Insurance companies is monitored by Insurance Regulatory and 
Development Authority (IRDAI). The engagement of Insurance companies under AB PM-JAY is 
monitored as per the contract signed between State Health Agencies and the Insurance 
Companies. NHA constantly shares feedback on the scheme implementation with the SHA. 
There is a dedicated dashboard for monitoring different parameters of scheme implementation 
related to insurance company.  
1.4.8 For mitigating the scope of unjustified profit making by the Insurance companies, 
provision has been made, where, in case the Insurer's average Claim Ratio falls below certain 
threshold, the insurance company is required to refund the premium paid after deducting the 
claims reimbursement amount and defined administrative expenditure. 
1.4.9 It is pertinent to note that the National Health Authority has set up a National Anti-Fraud 
Unit (NAFU) as the Anti-Fraud Cell at National and State level with the primary responsibility of 
prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under PM JAY. In addition, all 
States/UTs except Lakshadweep have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State level to 
instrumentalize anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level. The systems 
established by NAFU runs different kind of triggers to examine possible nexus between 
stakeholders to defraud the system facilitating timely action to prevent/deter the occurrence or 
penalise the defaulter. 
 
1.5 Empanelment of Hospitals and Management  
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee also noticed that the availability of EHCPs is not uniform across the 
country, and it is very low in some of the States. The Ministry, in coordination with State 
authorities, should make concerted efforts to encourage more private hospitals to get empanelled 
under the scheme in all the districts, particularly in regions with low density of EHCPs, and to 
eradicate disparities in the availability of EHCPs per lakh beneficiaries across various regions 
of the country. The IEC activities may be utilised robustly in efforts to empanel more hospitals. 
This would make affordable and quality treatment accessible to poor and vulnerable populations 
uniformly across the country, particularly in rural and remote areas, removing any regional 
disparity. 
(Para 2.5.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 

7 
 
1.5.2 As on 14.05.2024, a total of 29,387 hospitals including 12,464 private hospitals have been 
empanelled under the scheme, out of which more than 28,300 hospitals have been empanelled 
under AB PM-JAY in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Further, as on date, over 2,950 hospitals have been 
empanelled in the aspirational districts under the scheme. This has been done with the objective 
to ensure better accessibility to healthcare in the close vicinity of the beneficiaries’ residence.  
1.5.3 As on 01.05.2024, approximately 6.96 crore hospital admissions worth over ₹ 94,225 
crore have been authorised under the scheme. The percentage of hospital admissions authorised 
in the private sector by count and amount are 55% and 67% respectively. In view of the above, it 
can clearly be seen that the participation of private hospitals under PM-JAY is healthy. 
1.5.4 With regards to empanelling new hospitals, it may kindly be noted that NHA has 
developed guidelines for empanelment of hospitals under AB PM-JAY wherein hospitals are 
empanelled post physical verification and subject to fulfilment of certain minimum criteria. 
However, SHAs have been provided flexibility regarding the empanelment criteria due to varying 
situation of demand and supply, and unique geographical situations in different States. The 
process of hospital empanelment is overseen by the respective State Health Agencies.  
1.5.5 It is a matter of record that there is a disparity among the States regarding the availability 
of healthcare services. Though PM-JAY aims at catalysing the private investment in healthcare 
facilities, its mandate is limited to empanelling available hospitals. However, at the same time, 
NHA has been constantly encouraging States / UTs to empanel more hospitals under the scheme 
to ensure access to quality healthcare to all eligible beneficiaries. To further improve their 
participation, a two-pronged strategy has been adopted by NHA: 
1   Expanding the network of hospitals empanelled under PM-JAY: 
1.5.6 Public health and hospitals being a State subject, State Health Agencies (SHAs) are 
mandated with the responsibility of empanelling hospitals under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.  
1.5.7 In this context, NHA has also been continuously following up with prominent corporate 
hospital chains for empanelment under the scheme. Along with this, NHA has consulted various 
private medical associations including IMA in order to understand the challenges of the hospitals 
and solicit their participation under the scheme. Similar efforts have also been put by States / UTs 
as well. As a result, several top corporate hospitals have been empanelled under the PM-JAY 
scheme.  
2 Improving the participation of already empanelled hospitals 
1.5.8 In order to improve the participation of already empanelled hospitals, the following steps 
have been undertaken: 
a. Package rates have been revised under HBP 2022 in which package rates have increased 
for 350 packages and new packages have been added. 

8 
 
b. Claim settlement is being monitored at highest level and it is being ensured that claim is 
settled within defined turnaround time. 
c. Virtual and physical capacity building of hospitals are being undertaken. 
d. NHA has introduced a hospital-specific toll-free number (14413) to address the concerns 
of hospitals on a real-time basis. 
e. NHA have issued instructions to SHAs that DIUs should regularly visit empanelled 
hospitals to understand their concern and review their participation under the scheme.  
 
1.6  Convergence of PM-JAY with Schemes of States  
Recommendation 
1.6.1 The Committee observes that the PM-JAY scheme is running either after merging or in 
parallel with the State Government schemes. There are concerns that at the time of 
implementation, PMJAY, which is the major funding agency, may get the back seat in 
comparison to State schemes. The Government is taking steps like co-branding of Ayushman 
Bharat cards, kiosks, etc. The Committee believes that the Central Government should make 
efforts in right earnest for the convergence of State schemes with Ayushman Bharat and to give 
prominence to PMJAY.   
(Para 2.6.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.6.2 One of the core principles around which AB PM-JAY has been designed is to ensure 
appropriate convergence and uniformity of healthcare schemes in the country. This ensures 
comprehensive coverage for catastrophic illness, establish national standards for health assurance 
systems and provide national portability of the care.  
1.6.3 Over the years of implementation, 24 States/UTs have converged their State schemes with 
Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. However, in few smaller States, the State specific scheme has not 
been converged with PM-JAY. Efforts are being made to achieve the convergence of such 
schemes with PM-JAY. 
1.6.4 Further, many of these States have also agreed to issue co-branded Ayushman cards to all 
eligible beneficiaries (including State scheme beneficiaries). Also, uniform Hospital 
kiosk/Helpdesk are being setup in all hospitals empanelled under AB PM-JAY. These hospital 
kiosks have been designed and branded as per the IEC guidelines of NHA. The objective is to 
provide assistance to AB PM-JAY beneficiaries in beneficiary verification and issuance of 
Ayushman Card, availing treatment or any other support required by the beneficiaries. As on 
date, more than 9,500 Kiosks have been deployed. 
1.6.5 This has helped AB PM-JAY to be identified as a national scheme aimed at achieving the 
vision of free access to quality healthcare services to all. 

9 
 
1.7 Monitoring, Fraud Control and Grievance Redressal 
Recommendation 
1.7.1 The Committee appreciates the fact that during the study of this subject, about 98 percent 
of the total grievances registered were resolved and the implementation of PM-JAY is being 
continuously monitored and evaluated at NHA. The Committee endorses the need for a robust 
data collection and analysis system for a mega scheme. Further, fraudulent practices, such as 
overbilling and unnecessary procedures, can strain the program's finances and undermine its 
goals. Preventing and detecting fraud is a significant concern. In view of these facts, the 
Committee is of the opinion that technology is crucial for monitoring and fraud prevention, as all 
the processes and data are in electronic form. To enhance the evaluation and analysis of 
available data in PMJAY, the Committee recommends establishing a dedicated and skilled IT 
research team, to develop and monitor the technical aspects of IT applications for effective 
dissemination of information and data analysis. Additionally, regular upgrades and 
improvements to PM-JAY portals and modules are essential. Capacity-building programs in IT 
and data processing should be organised for officials and stakeholders, including hospital staff, 
at various levels.  
(Para 2.7.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.7.2 AB PM-JAY is implemented through an end-to-end IT enabled system. All the relevant 
data related to Ayushman card creation, hospital admission, claim processing, hospital 
empanelment, etc. are captured on a real time basis.  This helps in ensuring efficiency, 
transparency and accountability into the system. 
1.7.3 Along with this, it may kindly be noted that a dedicated monitoring & research team has 
been put in place which helps develop various types of analytical dashboards which monitor the 
status of the implementation of AB PM-JAY based on Key Performance Indicators and generate 
reports for the same. Analytical reports help identify trends with respect to beneficiary 
identification and claim management. Along with this, the team works on various working papers 
and policy briefs that pave way for evidence-based decision making under AB PM-JAY.   
1.7.4 National Health Authority has setup a National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) with the primary 
responsibility of prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under PM-JAY. Further, 
all States/UTs have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State level to instrumentalize 
anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level.  
 1.7.5 With respect to the upgrades in the system, it may kindly be noted that NHA has been 
using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to detect suspicious 
transactions / potential frauds in AB PM-JAY. Technologies deployed include rule-based triggers 
and Machine Learning algorithms, fuzzy logic, image classification and de-duplication, etc.  
NHA is also using fraud analytics services.  

10 
 
1.7.6  Further, NHA has collaborated with Insurance Institute of India for Joint Certification 
Course and training modules to enhance technical skills of Medical Auditors / Field Investigators. 
State wise Annual Training Calendar have been finalised and due training including training of 
trainers (ToTs) are given to the stakeholders as per their requirement. 
1.7.7  Some of the key initiatives undertaken by NHA for capacity building is as follows:  
● The Capacity Building division has meticulously mapped stakeholders to thematic areas, 
analysing the specific knowledge levels required by each stakeholder group. 
● An Annual Training Calendar has been prepared for the States and NHA based on the 
different stakeholders and inputs received from 33 States and UTs. 
● National Health Authority has designed a Learning Management System (LMS) known as 
Arogya Shiksha, which serves as a platform for managing, documenting, tracking, 
reporting, and delivering training sessions related to PM-JAY. This initiative intends to

1.8 Challenges and potential areas of improvement under PM-JAY  
Recommendation 
1.8.1 The Committee is of the considered view that to achieve Universal Health Coverage, 
untapped sections of community, regions and sections of the people must be covered under the 
scheme to increase the covered population axis. Providing preventive health and making the 
health benefit packages attractive would result in decrease in disease burden axis thereby 
reducing the implementation cost, the third axis of the Cube. Addressing these shortcomings 
requires a comprehensive approach, including strengthening healthcare infrastructure, 
improving administrative efficiency, enhancing awareness, and implementing robust monitoring 
mechanisms to ensure transparency and accountability.  
(Para 3.2.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 

13 
 
1.8.2 When Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri – Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) was 
launched in 2018, 10.74 crore beneficiary families were targeted based on the Socio-economic 
Caste Census (SECC) of 2011 using select deprivation and occupational criteria across rural and 
urban areas respectively to identify the families. Further, in January 2022, the Cabinet of the 
Government of India, revised the beneficiary base to 12 crore families. Many States/UTs 
implementing AB PM-JAY have further expanded the beneficiary base to approximately 18.4 
crore families, at their own cost. 
1.8.3 Further, the Government of India, in the interim budget for 2023-24, has announced the 
inclusion of about 37 lakh Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Anganwadi Workers 
(AWWs) and Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) across the country under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.  
1.8.4 Ayushman Bharat adopts a continuum of care approach, comprising two inter-related 
components, which are – HWC & PM-JAY.  
1.8.5 Health and Wellness Centers (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) are envisaged to deliver an 
expanded range of services to address the primary health care needs of the entire population in an 
area, expanding access, universality and equity close to the community. The emphasis of health 
promotion and prevention is designed to bring focus on keeping people healthy by engaging and 
empowering individuals and communities to choose healthy behaviours and make changes that 
reduce the risk of developing chronic diseases and morbidities. 
1.8.6 With respect to the rates and packages defined under PM-JAY, it is important to note that 
the Health Benefit packages used under AB PM-JAY have been revised and rationalized over the 
years. To begin with, AB PM-JAY initially had 1393 treatment packages. However, the fifth and 
the latest Health Benefit package - HBP 2022 was launched in April 2022 wherein a total of 365 
procedures have been added and rates have been revised upwards in case of 832 procedures. HBP 
2022 consists of 1949 procedures including 1 unspecified package across 27 specialities.  
 
1.9 Quality of Healthcare Services and health infrastructure  
Recommendation 
1.9.1 The Committee has been informed of the complaints regarding delays in settling claims 
and payments. This may be because schemes like PM-JAY deal in volume. The Government 
should address the issue by ensuring that the turnaround time of claim settlement and claim 
rejection ratio is reduced significantly. This may be done by implementing various provisions like 
the use of IT-based modules, regular interaction among SHAs, EHCPs, ISAs, insurance 
companies and other stakeholders, and capacity building of stakeholders involved in claim 
processing. These steps would increase the proportion of timely payments, which is the major 
concern of most hospitals and would attract major private hospitals for empanelment under PM-
JAY. 

14 
 
(Para 3.2.3(i) (b) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.9.2 Timely settlement of claims is one the key parameters against which scheme performance 
is measured. NHA has adopted multi-pronged strategy for timely settlement of claims which 
includes skill upgradation of adjudicators, process re-engineering, monitoring of fund release, etc. 
Some of the key initiatives include: 
1. NHA has collaborated with Insurance Institute of India for Joint Certification Course and 
training modules to enhance technical skills of Medical Auditors / Field Investigators.  
2. State wise Annual Training Calendar has been finalized and due training including

3. Discussions are held with States for timely release of State share of fund.  
4. Query process made more objective 
5. Clearly defined roles and responsibilities of claim adjudicators at different level 
6. NHA has launched another initiative called the Green Channel Payments (GCP) with the

7. NHA has also developed an analytical dashboard for more granular monitoring of claim 
adjudication under the scheme. 
 
Recommendation

healthcare infrastructure and services between different states and regions, which lead to 
unequal access and outcomes. Moreover, most of the healthcare infrastructure is concentrated in 
cities and urban areas. It is also seen that the public healthcare facilities available in rural areas 
are flawed due to the shortage of well-equipped and staffed infrastructure, which limits the 
accessibility to care. The Committee believes that the Government should take steps to strengthen 
the healthcare infrastructure in rural and underserved areas to ensure accessibility to quality 
healthcare services 
(Para 3.2.3(i) (c) of the Report)

1.9.4 As of 14th May, 2024, a total of 29,387 hospitals including 12 464 private hospitals have

15

1.10 Monitoring, Fraud Control and Grievance Redressal 
Recommendation 
1.10.1 The Committee would like to place an emphasis in applying behavioural science insights 
to increase the uptake of the PMJAY Scheme. Keeping in view some of the recent behavioural 
studies, the Committee suggests that PMJAY messaging to the targeted population can be revised 
by including the following behavioural insights: 
 Simplification: PMJAY messaging to contain short and simplified text with clear 
behavioural instruction to register with the Scheme. 
 Social norms: People simulate behaviour when they see that others are also doing it. 
PMJAY messaging can be designed in such a way that carries a strong message that 
others are doing it. Moreover, behavioural studies indicate that people are risk-seeking 
over losses but risk-averse over gains. Gain-framed PMJAY messaging will prove to be 
effective. 
(Para 3.2.3(i) (d) of the Report)

1.11 Importance to Medical Ethics 
Recommendation 
1.11.1 The Committee is of the opinion that maintaining medical ethics and avoiding 
unnecessary procedures, tests, and over-prescription is a concern, as it can lead to rising costs 
and potential harm to patients. The Government should give impetus to value education and 
ethics in medical curriculum and training workshops to sensitise the staff involved in the 
implementation of the scheme that maintaining small ethical standards would bring significant 
results. 
(Para 3.2.3(iii) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.11.2 For the treatments under PM-JAY, NHA has developed a total of 28 sets of 675 Standard 
Treatment Guidelines (STGs) in order to ensure appropriate healthcare delivery for specific 
clinical circumstances. STGs have been integrated in TMS for assisting adjudicators in 
processing of request for pre-authorizations and claims. 
1.11.3 Further, National Health Authority has setup a National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) with the 
primary responsibility of prevention, detection and deterrence of fraud and abuse under PM-JAY. 
Further, all States/UTs have set up State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFUs) at the State level to 
instrumentalize anti-fraud and abuse control activities at the ground level. 

17 
 
1.11.4 With respect to the upgrades in the system, it may kindly be noted that NHA has been 
using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to detect suspicious 
transactions / potential frauds in AB PM-JAY. Technologies deployed include rule-based triggers 
and Machine Learning algorithms, fuzzy logic, image classification and de-duplication, etc. 
1.11.5 The Government has taken significant steps to incorporate value education into medical 
curriculum and training programs. Section 25 (1)(b) of NMC Act, 2019 provides that Post-
Graduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB) under NMC develop competency based dynamic 
curriculum at postgraduate level and super-speciality level in accordance with the regulations 
made under this Act, with a view to develop appropriate skill, knowledge, attitude, values and 
ethics among postgraduates and super-specialists to provide healthcare, impart medical education 
and conduct medical research. 
1.11.6 In response to above quoted section, NMC Post Graduate Medical Education Regulations, 
2023 or “PGMER-23” in its abbreviated form, provides that all postgraduate students shall 
complete course in ethics including Good Clinical Practices and Good Laboratory Practices, 
whichever is relevant to them, to be conducted by Institutions/Universities. The students are 
expected to complete the course in the first year. No post-graduate student shall be permitted to 
appear in the examination without the above certification. Further, it shall be the duty of all 
concerned universities with the medical institutions under them, to partner with the NMC to 
provide training in clinical and practical skills along with theoretical knowledge, laying emphasis 
upon attitude, ethics and communication skills to ensure imparting competency-based medical 
education. 
 
1.12 Technology and Data Security 
Recommendation  
 
1.12.1 The Committee has been informed that the personal details and medical history of the 
beneficiaries under PMJAY are maintained by the NHA through various modules of their IT 
platform. The beneficiaries may visit multiple doctors. The digital record would help the doctor 
to see the medical history of the beneficiary with his/her consent. The NHA has also maintained a 
standardised registry containing the list of all the hospitals, which is called the Healthcare 
Facility Registry, a list of all the healthcare professionals, doctors, nurses, a list of all labs, a list 
of all the drugs, etc. These initiatives are significant to make the PMJAY scheme cashless, 
paperless, portable, transparent, etc. However, the Committee would also like to highlight that 
safeguarding patient data and ensuring the security of health information systems are vital to 
prevent data breaches and misuse. The Government must ensure robust IT infrastructure with 
quality encryption and safeguards. 
(Para 3.2.3 (iv) (a) of the Report) 

18 
 
Action Taken 
1.12.2 The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) aims to develop the backbone necessary 
to support the integrated digital health infrastructure of the country. It will bridge the existing gap 
amongst different stakeholders of healthcare ecosystem through digital highways. The Mission 
aims to create an integrated healthcare system that will link practitioners and patients digitally by 
giving them access to real-time health records. 
1.12.3 Under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission different registries are being created. Under 
ABDM, Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) is being created for every citizen, which 
shall work like her digital health-records wallet. Similarly, Healthcare Professionals Registry 
(HPR), a comprehensive repository of all healthcare professionals involved in delivery of 
healthcare services across both modern and traditional systems of medicine is being created. 
Further, Health Facility Registry (HFR) is a comprehensive repository of health facilities of the 
nation across different systems of medicine. It includes both public and private health facilities 
including hospitals, clinics, diagnostic laboratories and imaging centres, pharmacies, etc. As on 
16/05/2024, 61.46 crore ABHA cards have been created and 38.10 crore health records have been 
linked. Further, 2.67 lakh health facilities have been verified on HFR and 3.49 lakh healthcare 
professionals have been verified on HPR. 
1.12.4 Under AB PM-JAY, ABHA ID of the beneficiary has been integrated with PM-JAY ID to 
ensure seamless integration with larger healthcare ecosystem. 
1.12.5 National Health Authority (NHA) is committed to the protection of beneficiaries’ privacy 
and is taking the necessary steps to protect the personal data belonging to beneficiaries’ or any 
individual who is a part of Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY). 
1.12.6 The repository in which NHA stores data is RDBMS (Relational Database management 
System) which has been setup in the NHA data center. PII (Personal Identifiable Information) of 
the beneficiary is stored in RDBMS in encrypted format.  
1.12.7 NHA has also engaged Telecom Consultants of India Limited (TCIL) as Security 
Operation Center (SOC) which monitors security postures (alerts & incidents) of the cloud 
infrastructure. They also conduct Security Assessment of all NHA Apps. They use the Threat 
Intelligence tools to ensure all known threats are configured in the rules and IOCs informed by 
various security agencies are blocked immediately to secure NHA Infrastructure. NHA also has a 
team of security experts over and above the security experts of Master Service Provider & Cloud 
Service Provider, who tracks the performance of IT system. 
1.13       Technology and Data Security 
Recommendation  
 

19 
 
1.13.1 The Committee also believes that the Government should give impetus to trust-building 
campaigns as some of the beneficiaries may hesitate to join the scheme of misleading information 
regarding breaches of their personal and medical data security. The Committee has also been 
informed that some of the healthcare professionals have also raised data security concerns and 
are hesitating to register at the NHA registry. The Government must address these concerns 
through continuous interaction and trust-building initiatives. 
(Para 3.2.3 (iv) (b) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.13.2 Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is designed on the principle of privacy 
preserving federated data architecture that is essential for enhancing the  security  and  privacy  of  
the  personal  and  sensitive  information  of  the citizens while ensuring interoperability and 
technological flexibility and independence. Therefore, data is not centralized but rather stored 
within the hospitals/facilities where it originates. Health data is always created and stored by 
healthcare providers. ABDM only facilitates secure data exchange between the intended 
stakeholders on ABDM network after the patient’s consent. Consequently, the responsibility for 
implementing robust data security mechanisms also falls upon these hospitals/facilities, where the 
data is stored. 
1.13.3 Only the data collected for registries such as the ABHA registry, Healthcare Professional 
Registry, and Healthcare Facility Registry is stored centrally. This central storage is imperative as 
these datasets play a crucial role in ensuring interoperability, trust, identification, and establishing 
a single source of truth across various digital health systems. 
1.13.4 Data sharing is allowed based in compliance with the ABDM Health Data Management 
Policy (“HDM Policy”) which has the principle of “Security and Privacy by Design” for the 
protection of individuals’ personal digital health privacy at its core. It acts as a guidance 
document across the National Digital Health Ecosystem (NDHE) and sets out the minimum 
standards for data privacy protection that should be followed to ensure compliance with relevant 
and applicable law, rules and regulations. 
1.13.5 The importance of trust-building campaigns, especially considering potential 
misinformation surrounding data security breaches is acknowledged. Extensive IEC in the form 
of radio spots, print media and IRCTC website have been initiated and will be continued to 
address these concerns and communicating the privacy related safeguards in ABDM so that 
beneficiaries feel confident in participating in the ABDM. 
1.13.6 In the National Healthcare Provider Registry (NHPR), healthcare professionals grant 
consent for the visibility of their profiles (public display) during registration. Additionally, 
professionals have the option to choose which fields they wish to display publicly. Consequently, 
based on their consent, specific fields within their profile, such as mobile numbers or email 
addresses, may be visible or not visible in the public domain as per their preference. We 
understand that some healthcare professionals may also have reservations regarding data security, 

20 
 
and we are actively working to engage with them directly and/or through their professional 
associations to address their concerns.  
 
1.14 Indirect Cost and Expenditure Beyond the cover of ₹ 5 lakh 
Recommendation  
 
1.14.1 The Committee has seen that, while interacting with the beneficiaries of Ayushman 
Bharat, even if the beneficiaries are insured, they must bear the high indirect cost that might go 
beyond their ability to pay. To address the catastrophic financial burden on poor patients and to 
achieve the objective of PMJAY, the Government needs to cover this indirect financial loss for a 
poor patient for whom this cost is not negligible. 
(Para 3.2.3(v) (a) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.14.2 AB PM-JAY provides health cover of up to ₹ 5 lakh per family per year for secondary 
and tertiary care hospitalization. The treatment packages under AB PM-JAY are very 
comprehensive which includes pre-hospitalization expenses including diagnostics, 
premedication, pre-anaesthetic examination, and consultation relevant to the present disease for 
up to 3 days and the package amount also covers post-hospitalization expenses including drug 
expenses for up to 15-days under this scheme. 
1.14.3 However, few States and UTs provide additional benefits in terms of transport allowance 
etc. to the scheme beneficiaries with the intent to reduce OOPE. 
1.14.4 The suggestions of the Committee regarding covering indirect expenses are noted.  
 
1.15 Indirect Cost and Expenditure Beyond the Cover of ₹ 5 lakhs 
 
Recommendation  
 
1.15.1 The Committee, while interacting with both private and government hospitals, has noted 
that some of the complex and high-end surgeries or chronic treatment cost more than the sum of 
₹ 5 lakhs covered under the PMJAY. Also, some of the costly procedures and surgeries are not 
covered under the scheme. To address such issues, some of the hospitals have set an example by 
successfully attracting Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds and private investment to 
create funds to bear the expenditure of beneficiaries for the cost of treatment over and above the 
insured sum of ₹ 5 lakhs. The Government need to implement such practices across the country 
to make PM-JAY more and more effective and beneficial for the poor sections of the society. 
Further, in many cases, the amount of ₹ 5 lakhs may not be utilised by every patient/family. Only 
in cases of serious diseases and other surgeries, this amount is utilised. Apart from Rashtriya 

21 
 
Arogya Nidhi, the Government should consider the creation of some special purpose vehicle or 
arrangement to cater to fill the gap in such special cases in a more structured manner. 
(Para 3.2.3 (v) (b) of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.15.2 With regard to the limit of ₹ 5 lakhs, it may be noted that 99.4% of expenditure incurred 
per treatment cycle is usually below ₹ 2 lakhs. Therefore, almost all treatments are covered under 
AB PM-JAY and the existing wallet of ₹ 5 lakhs is sufficient for providing treatment to the 
beneficiaries. Currently, PMJAY covers 1949 procedures across 27 specialities. High-end 
treatments like bone marrow transplant, renal transplant, medical and radiation oncology are 
covered under AB PM-JAY. 
1.15.3 Further, under Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN), eligible beneficiaries are provided higher 
cover for identified treatment. 
1.15.4 Further, few States have decided to expand the benefit cover under the scheme. Further, 
few SHAs have created a corpus using certain percentage of the claim revenues earned under by 
Government hospitals under the scheme to provide additional support for high end treatment 
beyond 5 lakhs. 
1.15.5 In view of the above, treatment requirement of the beneficiaries is mostly met. However, 
suggestion of the Committee is noted.
