release, and Real-time System of Integrated Quick Transfers (SNA SPARSH) 
compliance delays, the Department should establish a dedicated task force to provide 
intensive, institutionalised support to each state and union territory. This task force will 
conduct pre-emptive assessments of state needs, offer hands-on assistance with SNA 
SPARSH compliance, and facilitate timely release of state matching funds through 
regular communication and problem-solving workshops. Furthermore, the Department 
should implement a quarterly review system that incorporates direct feedback from 
states, allowing for real-time adjustments to funding allocations and program 
implementation. This approach will not only address the immediate issue of 
underutilization but also build stronger collaborative relationships with states, ensuring 
the long-term success of expanding medical education infrastructure and increasing the 
availability of medical professionals.

4.8 AYUSHMAN BHARAT-PRADHAN MANTRI JAN AROGYA YOJANA (AB-
PMJAY) 
 
4.8.1  Ayushman Bharat- Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is a 
flagship scheme of the Government which provides health cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per family per 
year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization to approximately 55 Cr beneficiaries 
corresponding to 12.37 Crore families constituting economically vulnerable bottom 40% of 
India’s population. AB-PMJAY aims to expand service availability across the country by 
empaneling not only public but also private healthcare facilities. AB-PMJAY provides 
significant flexibility by allowing states to choose the mode of implementation, packages 
offered, package pricing and reservation according to their level of development and stage of 
epidemiological transition. The scheme provides cashless and paperless inpatient Secondary 
and Tertiary medical care in public as well as private empanelled hospitals. The scheme 
covers 1961 procedures across 27 medical specialties through a network of 30,201 
empanelled Public and Private Hospitals.  
 
4.8.2  The key objectives of the scheme have been informed as follows:  
 
i) Address unmet health needs: Actively identifying and taking steps to provide 
necessary healthcare services to beneficiaries who currently lack access to 
adequate treatment due to factors like availability, affordability or awareness 
of required care, etc.  
ii) Comprehensive coverage: Ensure coverage for a wide range of illnesses 
iii) Financial protection: Reduce catastrophic health expenditures 
iv) Healthcare accessibility: Enhance access to healthcare facilities across the 
country 
v) Ensure adaptability: Empowers states to adapt implementation based on local 
needs, including various health insurance/assurance schemes in the states/UTs. 
 
 
4.8.3  With respect to the scheme uptake the Department submitted that AB-PMJAY 
has been implemented since September, 2018. Over the last 5 years of scheme

Recently, the scheme has been expanded to cover 6 crore senior citizens of age 70 years and 
above belonging to 4.5 crore families under AB-PMJAY Vay Vandana scheme, irrespective 
of their socio economic status. As on date, except for West Bengal, all the States across the 
nation have been on-boarded under AB-PMJAY. The Department submitted the details on

4.8.6  On a specific query, the Department submitted information on its projection to

undertaking several IEC activities to create beneficiary awareness under the scheme. 
 
4.8.7  The Committee is of the opinion that the Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan 
Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is a pivotal and visionary health initiative 
aiming to provide financial protection and healthcare access to a large number of 
India's vulnerable population. While the scheme has seen substantial growth in terms of 
state participation, card creation, and hospital admissions, several key areas require 
attention like Budget Utilization and State Participation. The Committee observes a 

144 
 
persistent trend of underutilization of allocated funds, particularly in the previous year 
as well as in the current financial year. The Committee observes that, in the FY 2023-24, 
an amount of Rs. 7200.00 crore was allocated as BE 2023-24 which was reduced to Rs. 
6800.00 crore at RE stage, however, the actual expenditure was Rs. 6670.47 crore.  In 
the FY 2024-25, Rs. 7300.00 crores was made in BE 2024-25 which was revised to Rs. 
7605.54 crores at RE 2024-25, however, the actual expenditure was to the tune of Rs. 
5034.03 Crores till 09.01.2025. In FY 2025-26, the enhanced amount of Rs. 9406 crore 
has been allocated as BE 2025-26.  This indicates potential inefficiencies in fund 
disbursement or implementation bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends a 
thorough review of the fund release mechanisms to states/UTs. This review should focus 
on identifying and eliminating bottlenecks that contribute to underutilization. 
Specifically, the Department should implement a system of proactive monitoring of fund 
utilization by states, coupled with targeted support to address any implementation 
challenges. This support could include technical assistance, capacity building, and 
simplified reporting procedures. Furthermore, the committee suggests that the release of 
funds be linked to the performance of states in terms of card creation, hospital 
admissions, and beneficiary feedback, ensuring that funds are directed to areas of 
greatest need and impact. The Department should also create and publish a clear and 
concise guideline for states, explaining the process of fund requests, and the expected 
timelines. To ensure that the allocation of fund to the tune of Rs. 9406.00 crore in BE 
2025-26 is utilized, a quarterly review system may be set up to avoid any delays in 
release of fund to States/UTs. 
 
4.8.8  The Committee is of the view that besides the large number of empanelled 
hospitals and issuance of cards, the crucial factor for successful implementation of the 
Yojana in public awareness about the Yojana is public awareness about the Yojana. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends a focused campaign, high-level engagement with the 
respective state governments, addressing their specific concerns and highlighting the 
benefits of the scheme for their populations. The Department should intensify its efforts 
to enhance beneficiary awareness, particularly in rural and underserved areas. This can 
be achieved through targeted Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) 
campaigns, utilizing local languages and community-based approaches. Leveraging 
ASHA and Anganwadi workers, as well as digital platforms, to disseminate information 
and facilitate card creation is crucial. The Committee also recommends that the 
Department conduct regular beneficiary feedback surveys to assess the effectiveness of 
awareness campaigns and identify areas for improvement. A dedicated helpline and 
easily accessible grievance redressal mechanism should also be established to address 
beneficiary concerns promptly. Further, public displays of information regarding 
hospital empanelment and available procedures should be made mandatory at all public 
health centers. 
 
4.8.9  The Committee appreciates that the Government has recently expanded 
the AB-PMJAY to cover 6 crore senior citizens of age 70 years and above belonging to 
4.5 crore families under AB-PMJAY Vay Vandana scheme, irrespective of their socio 
economic status. The Committee observes that an amount to the tune of Rs. 1443.00 

145 
 
crore has been earmarked for treatment of senior citizens of the age of 70 years and 
above holding Ayushman Vay Vandna Cards.  The Committee is of the view that age 
criteria of 70 years and above for Ayushman Vay Vandna Cards should be rationalized 
to 60 years and above irrespective of their socio-economic status for widening the 
coverage of the scheme in the better interest of common masses. 
 
4.8.10  The Committee also recommends the Department to launch public 
awareness campaign about AB-PMJAY so that intended beneficiaries of the Yojana are 
not left out from coverage. 
 
4.8.11  The Committee, keeping in view huge expenditure on the critical 
healthcare, should revise healthcare coverage from existing Rs. 5 lakh per family per 
year to Rs. 10 lakh per family per year.  
 
4.8.12   The Committee observes that several high-end interventions/procedures, 
and even high-end diagnostics are not included in AB-PMJAY. The Committee 
recommends that the number of packages/procedures covered under the Yojana should 
be reviewed and the fresh packages/procedures related to treatment of critical illness 
with high cost of treatment and expensive high-end investigations/diagnostics like 
radiological diagnostics (CT, MRI, imaging including Nuclear Imaging) be incorporated 
in AB-PMJAY instead of leaving the same to be booked as Add-on packages.  
 
4.8.13   The Committee has come across the instances of delay in settlement of 
claims of empanelled hospitals under AB-PMJAY and that the package rates have not 
been reasonably revised in many States resulting into inconvenience caused to the 
patients due to denial of treatment by many empanelled hospitals. The Committee, 
therefore, considers that the States/UTs which have not revised the package rates may 
be persuaded by the Department to revise the package rates on the similar lines of rates 
revised by some of the States in 2022. In addition to the above, the Committee 
recommends that the Department review and streamline the process related to 
settlement of claims submitted by the empanelled hospitals within the specified time.  
 
4.8.14  The Committee has been given to understand that the operational period 
of National Health Mission (NHM) is from FY 2021 to FY 2026, therefore, coming to an 
end on 31.03.2026. The Committee, considering the pivotal significance of the Mission, is

Mission.

5.8 ISSUANCE OF ABHA CARDS 
5.8.1  On discussion related to issuance of ABHA Cards on the basis of 2011 census, 
the Department informed the Committee that ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) is a 
unique health ID under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), which focuses on 
creating a digital health ecosystem. ABDM was launched on 27 Sep 2021. It enables 
individuals to access and share their health records securely with their consent. However, 
ABDM does not provide any financial health coverage or insurance. Ayushman Bharat 
Pradhan Mantri - Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is a scheme which provides health cover 
of Rs. 5 lakhs per eligible beneficiary family per year for secondary and tertiary care 
hospitalization. Under AB PM-JAY initially, 10.74 crore eligible households were identified 
under the scheme from SECC 2011 based on certain deprivation and occupational criteria in 
rural and urban areas respectively. Further, in January 2022, the Government of India revised 
the beneficiary base to 12 crore families, considering the decadal population growth rate of 
11.7% and gave the flexibility to States/UTs to use other databases of schemes meant for 
similar socio-economic profile which are Aadhaar verified. In March 2024, 37 lakh families 
of Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and 
Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) were also included in the scheme. Further, on 29th October 
2024, the Government has expanded AB PM-JAY to provide free treatment benefits of up to 
₹5 lakh per year to all senior citizens aged 70 years and above along with their families, 
irrespective of their socio-economic status. 
 
5.8.2  The Committee notes the expansion of coverage from different segments 
of population under AB-PMJAY scheme from time to time, however, the Committee 
recommends the Department for  the immediate and consistent integration of updated 
demographic data into the ABHA card issuance and PMJAY beneficiary identification 
processes. Specifically, while the PMJAY scheme has made efforts to expand its 
coverage beyond the 2011 census, the fundamental reliance on outdated data for initial 
identification and ABHA card linkage creates potential exclusion and inaccuracy. This 
continuous updating will ensure that the schemes remain relevant and equitable, 
reflecting the true health needs of the population.

5.9 AYUSHMAN BHARAT- TRIBAL AREAS AND MIGRANT POPULATION 
 
5.9.1  On the issues of Ayushman Bharat in tribal areas not effective because of 
migrating population and lack of blood storage facility in PHCs and gynaecologists in rural 
and tribal areas, the Department apprised of the Committee that AB-PMJAY has a unique 
feature called ‘portability’ and under this feature, eligible beneficiaries can access healthcare 
services at any empanelled hospital across the country irrespective of their place of residence. 
This feature is especially beneficial for migrant workers. Further, NHA is actively working on 
reaching out to eligible beneficiaries through a massive IEC campaign and Ayushman Card 
creation drive. In this direction, initiatives like Aapke Dwar Ayushman campaign have been 
undertaken by NHA since January 2021 which enlisted the services of grassroots 
functionaries for beneficiary mobilization and card creation. Aapke Dwar Ayushman 2.0 was 
launched in 2022 which resulted in approximately 10 crore Ayushman cards created during 
2022-23 and 11.58 crore cards during 2023-24. Now, Aapke Dwar Ayushman 3.0 campaign 
has been relaunched with Self-registration feature enabling beneficiaries to create Ayushman 
card for himself/herself along with his/her family. Special card drives were also being 
undertaken under Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyaan (PM- JANMAN), 
Viksit Bharat Sankalp Yatra (VBSY), Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Unnat Gram Abhiyan (PM-
JUGA) Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan etc. for card creation. Further field level 
workers like ASHA, Anganwadi Worker and Anganwadi Helpers are also incentivized for 
creation of Ayushman Cards. As on date, more than 36.58 Crore Ayushman Cards have been 
created under the scheme. Further, NHA has issued directions to the States/UTs to undertake 
extensive IEC activities to raise awareness about the scheme. 
5.9.2  The Committee is of the view that initiatives like "Aapke Dwar 
Ayushman" campaign should not be confined to creation of Ayushman Cards as 
highlighting vast number of creation of card is not the only objective of the scheme. 
Rather the Department should make efforts to ensure establishing robust healthcare 
infrastructure and service delivery in tribal and rural areas. While the portability 
feature and card creation drives are valuable, the core issue remains the lack of essential 
medical facilities like blood storage in PHCs, and availability of specialists like 
gynaecologists, particularly in regions with migrating populations. Therefore, the 
Committee urges upon the co-ordination between different components of the 
Ayushman Bharat scheme. The National Health Authority (NHA) should integrate these 
critical healthcare components with the "Aapke Dwar Ayushman" framework. This 
would entail deploying mobile medical units equipped with basic ICU facilities, blood 
storage capabilities, and specialist services like gynaecology to remote areas during the 
campaign. Additionally, the campaign should facilitate the establishment of sustainable 
blood collection and storage systems at PHCs and prioritize the recruitment and 
deployment of specialists like gynaecologists to these underserved regions, to bridge the 
gap between awareness and accessible, comprehensive healthcare delivery.

5.10 GIG WORKERS UNDER PMJAY SCHEME 
5.10.1  On being asked about the roadmap/plan to cover Gig workers under PMJAY 
Scheme, the Department informed that to successfully extend AB-PMJAY benefits to 10 
million gig workers, the initial step is to identify eligible beneficiaries and regularly update 
the dynamic database of eligible gig workers. Since AB-PMJAY relies on an Aadhaar-seeded 
database for verification and enrolment, it is essential to ensure seamless integration with the 
E-Shram portal, where gig workers will be registered under the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment (MoLE). Additionally, to enhance efficiency and minimize exclusions, NHA is 
taking up the matter with MoLE for identified following steps: - 
i. Data Integration: Establish a real-time data-sharing mechanism between the E-
Shram portal and the AB PM-JAY database to streamline verification. 
ii. Awareness and Outreach: Conduct awareness campaigns to encourage gig workers 
to register on the E-Shram portal and update their Aadhaar details. 
iii. Collaboration with Platforms: Engage with gig economy platforms (such as 
delivery and ride-hailing services) to ensure their workers are registered under E-
Shram. 
 
5.10.2  The Committee, to ensure the effective inclusion of 10 million gig workers 
under the PMJAY scheme, recommends the Department for immediate establishment of 
a dedicated, automated, and real-time data synchronization system between the E-
Shram portal and the AB-PMJAY database. This system should be designed to facilitate 
seamless, continuous, and error-free data transfer, enabling instant verification and de-
duplication exercise to identify and eliminate any overlap. This focused approach to 
data integration, alongside the planned awareness campaigns and platform 
collaborations, will minimize enrollment delays and ensure that all eligible gig workers 
receive timely access to essential healthcare benefits, while preventing double counting 
of beneficiaries. 
5.11 COVERAGE OF OPD SERVICES AND COST OF MEDICINE UNDER THE 
AYUSHMAN BHARAT 
5.11.1  On being enquired about the coverage of OPD services and cost of medicine 
under the Ayushman Bharat under PMJAY Scheme, the Department made a submission that 
AB-PMJAY provides health cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per eligible beneficiary family per year for 
secondary and tertiary care for in-patient care only i.e. hospitalization. OPD services are not 
covered under the scheme however, certain day care packages are included in the package 
master of the scheme like surgery for cataract, dialysis, animal bites etc. Further, the treatment 
packages under the scheme are comprehensive and includes pre-hospitalization expenses 
including diagnostics, pre-medication, pre-anesthetic examination, and consultation relevant 
to the present disease for up to 3 days and the package amount also covers post-
hospitalization expenses including medicine expenses for up to 15-days under this scheme.   
5.11.2  The Committee recommends the phased inclusion of essential OPD 
services and a broader range of post-hospitalization medication coverage within the 

154 
 
Ayushman Bharat PMJAY scheme. While acknowledging the scheme's focus on 
secondary and tertiary inpatient care, the current exclusion of routine OPD services and 
limited post-hospitalization medication coverage creates a significant gap in accessible 
healthcare. To ensure continuity and build upon the existing framework, the 
recommendation should propose a phased approach, starting with the inclusion of 
essential OPD services for chronic diseases and commonly reported ailments. 
Furthermore, extending post-hospitalization medication coverage beyond the current 
15-day limit, particularly for conditions requiring prolonged treatment, would 
significantly reduce the financial burden on beneficiaries while addressing a need for 
comprehensive healthcare access. 
5.12 MISUSE OF FUND UNDER AB-PMJAY SCHEME 
5.12.1  The Committee expresses concern over misuse under AB-PMJAY scheme 
through fraudulent activities by some hospitals as a business model, and requirement of 
necessary regulation to check the same. The Department replied that NHA has adopted a zero-
tolerance policy towards fraud and abuse and has been taking steps for prevention, detection, 
and deterrence of different kinds of fraud that could occur in AB-PMJAY at different stages 
of its implementation. National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU) has been established at NHA and 
works in close coordination with State Anti-Fraud Units (SAFU) to investigate and take joint 
action against issues related to fraud and abuse. Suitable actions including de-empanelment of 
hospitals (1113), levying penalty on errant hospitals (1504) worth Rs 122 Cr, and suspension 
of hospitals (596) have been taken against fraudulent entities as reported by the States/UTs. 
 
5.12.2  With regard to the State of Gujarat, the Department stated that suitable penal 
actions have been undertaken against hospitals and doctors involved in malpractices under the 
scheme. As on date, a total of 9 doctors and 71 hospitals have been suspended under the 
scheme. Additionally, 2 hospitals have been de-empanelled, and 1 hospital has been 
blacklisted. Further, as part of the enforcement measures, financial recoveries and penalties 
have also been imposed to deter further violations. A total recovery of ₹15.08 crore has been 
made, while penalties amounting to ₹19.90 crore have been imposed. 
 
5.12.3  Further, guidelines have been issued for medical camps conducted by 
empanelled hospitals under AB-PMJAY, mandating prior intimation to the district health 
officer, the presence of a government medical officer, and prohibiting enrolment activities. 
Additionally, new state-specific triggers have been implemented to enhance oversight. To 
further curb misuse and abuse of the scheme, additional pre-investigation documents have 
been made mandatory for pre-authorization in cardiology and pediatric procedures. 
 
5.12.4  The Committee recommends the National Health Authority (NHA) 
implement a proactive, data-driven, and transparent monitoring system focusing on 
early detection of potential misuse patterns in AB-PMJAY. This system should go 
beyond reacting to reported fraud by continuously analyzing claim data, hospital 
activity, and patient feedback to identify statistical anomalies and emerging trends 
indicating potential abuse. Specifically, the NHA should develop and publicly report on 

155 
 
key performance indicators related to fraud detection, including the frequency of pre-
authorization requests for specific procedures, the ratio of medical camp referrals to 
hospital admissions, and the rates of hospital de-empanelment and penalties by state. In 
the collection and analysis of statistical data and feedback, the extensive use of AI and 
digital tools should be considered upon by the Department. This transparent, data-
driven approach will not only allow for quicker intervention but also serve as a 
deterrent, ensuring the scheme's resources are used for their intended purpose and 
maintaining public trust.  
 
5.13 PRADHAN MANTRI NATIONAL DIALYSIS PROGRAMME (PMNDP) 
5.13.1  The Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP) was launched in 
FY 2016-17 with the objective of having a dialysis centre in all district hospitals across India. 
The program includes provisions for scaling up of dialysis services to lower facilities up to 
the Community Health Centre level, based on the chronic kidney disease load and saturation 
of district hospitals. Under the PMNDP, State has to have One centre at DH level, however 
provision are there for expansion, if services have reached its saturation level. This expansion 
has to be decided by the State after reviewing the status. 
 
5.13.2  PMNDP is implemented in 36 States/UTs, covering 748 districts with 1,594 
HD centres and 11,011 HD machines as on 31st January, 2025. A portal launched in May 
2022 integrates all dialysis centres nationwide. In 2024, 60,489 BPL and 16,976 APL patients 
were registered for dialysis services. Under PMNDP Dialysis services are free for patients 
who are Below Poverty Line (BPL) but for other patients too services are available at the 
subsidized rates. The PMNDP portal has facility to register the Below Poverty Level (BPL) 
and Above Poverty Level (APL) financial status based on the entitlement card issued by the 
States /UTs at the time of new patient registration.  A total of 60,489 BPL patients have been 
registered in the portal. 
 
5.13.3  The Committee is of the view that the Dialysis facility under PMNDP 
should be given to the needy persons. The facility is being availed by persons who can 
afford treatment from their own pocket in private hospitals. The scheme provisions need 
to be reviewed. The Committee finds that the dialysis centres are at the District level at 
present, however, the Committee desires the Department should make strategy for 
setting up of  Dialysis facility at the Taluka level also as kidney patients are increasing.

5.15 HUB & SPOKE MODEL FOR CARDIAC AND STROKE  
5.15.1  The National Programme for Non-Communicable Diseases (NPNCD) focuses 
on strengthening infrastructure, human resource development, health promotion & awareness 
generation for prevention, early diagnosis, management and referral to an appropriate level of 
healthcare facility for treatment of the Non-Communicable Diseases. For effective 
management of patients with ST Segment Elevated Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) and 
Stroke, Hub and Spoke model is advised. States have to identify the Tertiary care hospitals as 
‘Hub’ based on infrastructure, experts and laboratory and intervention services and Spokes for 
early interventions. The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare provides support for stroke 
prevention and control under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-
Communicable Diseases. 
 

157 
 
5.15.2  NCD screening are integral component of NPNCD programme. Currently for 
population above 30 years plus as well as opportunistic screening are being undertaken for 
NCDs like Diabetes, Hypertension, Oral cancer, Breast cancer and cervical cancers. A 
nationwide National campaign is also being launched from 20th Feb 2025. 
 
5.15.3  The Committee endorses the views of Department for strengthening 
infrastructure, human resource development, health promotion & awareness generation 
for prevention, early diagnosis, management and referral to an appropriate level of 
healthcare facility for treatment of the Non-Communicable Diseases. The Committee 
desires that for effective management of patients with ST Segment Elevated Myocardial 
Infarction (STEMI) and Stroke, Hub and Spoke model may be implemented. The 
Department may persuade the States have to identify the Tertiary care hospitals as 
‘Hub’ based on infrastructure, experts and laboratory and intervention services and 
Spokes for early interventions.  
 
5.15.4  The Committee understands that NCD screening are integral component 
of NPNCD programme, therefore, the population aged 30 years and above must be 
undertaken for screening of NCDs like Diabetes, Hypertension, Oral cancer, Breast 
cancer and cervical cancers under National campaign launched from 20th Feb 2025. 
 
5.16 TRAUMA AND EMERGENCY CARE SERVICES 
5.16.1  A programme was started on pilot mode under the 9 th & 10th Five Year Plan 
(FYP) as “Pilot Project for strengthening emergency facilities along the highways”. During 
11th Plan, the programme was named as “Assistance for capacity building for developing 
trauma care facilities in Govt. hospitals on National Highways”. 116 Trauma Care Facilities 
were created under the scheme. 
 
5.16.2  During 12th plan, the scheme was extended as “Capacity building for 
developing Trauma Care Facilities in Govt. Hospitals on National Highways”, and 80 new 
trauma care facilities were created. Total 196 Trauma Care Facilities have been sanctioned. 
Further, “Pilot Programme for Prevention of Burn Injuries” (PPPBI) was approved during 
11th FYP. 9 Burns Units were created. During 12th FYP, the scheme was continued as 
“National Programme for Prevention & Management of Burn Injuries”. Total, 47 burn 
units have been sanctioned. Beyond 12th plan, there is no provision of identification of new 
trauma care facilities and the scheme was extended till March, 14 2020 and subsequently up 
to March, 2021. The Programme “NPPMT&BI” continues beyond 12th Five Year Plan and 
has been approved under the umbrella Scheme-Tertiary Care Programme from 2021-22 to 
2025-26. The financial support is in terms of release of the balance share of Central assistance 
within the total approved cost of the approved facilities during the 11th and 12th FYP. 
  
5.16.3  The Committee understands that NPPMT&BI scheme aims at reducing 
the mortality and morbidity occurring due to injuries (including trauma and burns), by 

158 
 
developing a system of services at pre- hospital & hospital level and continuum of care 
through rehabilitation. The Committee desires that adequate funds may be allocated for 
Trauma and Emergency Care Services to achieve the significant goals of the scheme that 
includes creating center of excellence from trauma and Burn Care in existing 
Government Medical Colleges. 
5.17 HIGH MALARIA CASES IN KOKRAJHAR, ASSAM 
5.17.1  On being enquired about the action taken to contain the high Malaria cases in 
Kokrajhar, Assam (especially in Bhutan Border areas), the Department submitted that as per 
the data available with National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) of the 
MoHFW, there were 3,808 malaria cases and 4 cases of deaths due to malaria reported in 
Kokrajhar district in Assam till December 2024, wherein all 4 blocks of Kokrajhar districts 
have reportedly witnessed an increase in cases in 2024, with the majority of cases from the 
northern part of the district. 
5.17.2  The Department submitted that the following actions have been taken to 
contain the disease: - 
 
i. The district administration and health authorities launched emergency 
interventions, including enhanced vector control measures and public 
awareness campaigns. 
ii. With the technical guidance of the NCVBDC tam, the State team 
immediately conducted field visits to the affected area for ensuring 
supportive supervision and monitoring of ongoing activities. 
iii. The Central Teams (Senior Regional Director, Guwahati and NCVBDC) 
conducted field visits on December 2 and during December 25-28, 2024 and 
observed that the majority of cases are concentrated in remote, forested areas. 
It was recommended to intensify surveillance and implement programme 
activities throughout the year, along with improving Long Lasting 
Insecticidal Net(LLIN_ distribution expanding Indoor Residual Spraying 
(IRS) coverage, and enhancing capacity building for field workers. 
Accordingly, LLINs distribution was initiated and IRS planned for the 
district. 
iv. All antimalarial and RDT kits were made available in sufficient quantities in 
all health facilities. 
v. State government was advised to devise and implement a concrete and robust 
monitoring mechanism to ensure follow-up for treatment completion for 
malaria positive cases. 
vi. While 34,268 LLINs were distributed in the Kokrajhar district, the State 
Government has been required to ensure proper usage of LLINs, conduct 
timely IRS activities by following correct procedure, and implement fogging 
in high transmission area. 
5.17.3  The Committee expresses concern that all 4 blocks of Kokrajhar districts 
have reportedly witnessed an increase in cases in 2024, with the majority of cases from 

159 
 
the northern part of the district. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
the Department should persuade the State Government to undertake concrete steps for 
combating the menace of malaria in Kokrajhar district, at the earliest. The Committee 
further recommends that the Department must ensure strengthening of treatment 
follow-up and capacity building mechanism of healthcare professionals to eliminate 
malaria from the country. 
5.18 PUBLIC PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP (PPP) MODEL FOR PROMOTING 
MEDICAL TOURISM 
5.18.1  As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the 
subject matter of 'Development and Promotion of Tourism' is allocated to the Ministry of 
Tourism. As such, the matter of boosting Medical Tourism falls under the purview of 
Ministry of Tourism. Additionally, the Ministry of External Affairs handles the ‘Medical and 
Ayush Visa Portal’ launched to streamline and regulate entry of genuine foreigners and 
ensure that only genuine hospitals are inviting the genuine patients for treatment by pre-
validating Medical Visa. This portal enables hospitals, on-board the portal ‘Medical and 
Ayush Visa Portal’, to generate Medical Visa invitation Letter and Medical Visa Extension 
Letter for Medical Visa/Medical Attendant Visa/Ayush Attendant Visa using the following 
URL: https://indianfrro.gov.in/frro/medicalvaluetravel. The pre-validation of Medical Visa is 
pre requisite to acquire Medical Visa and Medical Visa will be issued after pre-validation. 
 
5.18.2  The Committee understands that the promotion of medical tourism 
requires multi-disciplinary and multi-pronged approach, thereby seeks the involvement 
of Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of External Affairs but no one can exclude the 
pivotal role of the Department of Health and Family Welfare because the subject health 
where upon the focus is to be made for promoting medical tourism. The Committee 
perceives that the rate of medical tourism growth is much higher than the normal 
tourism growth, therefore the role of the Department of Health and Family Welfare is of 
pivotal importance. The Committee observes that growth of medical tourism in private 
sector is better than the public sector, therefore, there is enormous scope for promoting 
medical tourism in public sector. The Committee further recommends that the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare, in tandem with the Ministry of Tourism and 
the Ministry of External Affairs, leave no stone unturned in emphasising Public Private 
Partnership (PPP) model for promoting medical tourism.  
5.19 ACCESSSIBLE AND AFFORDABLE  TREATMENT OF RARE DISEASES 
5.19.1  The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has formulated National Policy for 
Rare Diseases (NPRD), 2021. As per the policy, Rare Diseases are categorized into three 
groups: - 
 
a. Rare diseases requiring one time curative and definitive treatment (e.g. Disorders 
amenable with Hematopoietic stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) and organ 
transplantation). 

160 
 
b. Rare Diseases requiring life-long treatment with good response on therapy: (e.g. 
Phenylketonuria, tyrosinemia type-1 and 2, Maple Syrup Urine Disease, Prader Willi 
Syndrome etc.) 
c. Rare Diseases requiring life-long disease stabilization and prolongation of life is only 
possible (only ambulatory improvement): e.g. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Spinal 
Muscular Atrophy, Pompe Disease, Gaucher’s Disease, Cystic Fibrosis etc.). 
 
5.19.2  As per NPRD, 2021, 13 Centres of Excellence have been identified, which are 
premier Government tertiary hospitals for diagnosis, prevention and treatment of rare 
diseases. Currently, 63 Rare Diseases are covered under the policy. However, this list is not 
exhaustive and is reviewed periodically based on the recommendations of Central Technical 
Committee for Rare Diseases (CTCRD). 
 
5.19.3  The Committee notes that 63 rare diseases are covered under National 
Policy for Rare Diseases (NPRD) which of course needs to be reviewed and expanded 
from time to time. In order to make the treatment of rare diseases accessible and 
affordable, the Department may make provision for cheaper diagnosis, prevention and 
treatment. The Committee also desires that the Department should launch national 
campaign/awareness programme for seeking treatment of the rare diseases.  
5.20 OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE  
(i) The sanctioning of Medical colleges should be on the basis of population and not 
district-wise as this creates imbalance in Hospital to population ratio. Moreover, the 
quality of Medicine and Nursing education should be as per National Quality Assurance 
Standards (NQAS) and the global best practices;  
(ii) Private medical education should be made cheaper and the Capitation fees needs 
to be regulated to make the medical education more affordable and accessible to merit 
candidates with poor financial background; 
(iii) Expediting the process of consideration of HPV vaccine roll-out plan and 
bringing the same under the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP); 
(iv) Making availability of Doctors at PHC/CHC level and lucrative pay and perks 
for specialist doctors ensuring their retention in the Government Hospitals. Department 
may persuade the States/UTs to overcome the shortage of doctors at PHCs/CHCs 
through various measures including the creation of separate Medical Services 
Recruitment Boards, specialist cadres, and providing flexibilities under NHM for 
recruitment and retention; 
(v) Provision of sufficient staff, essential diagnostics and quality generic medicines 
must be made available in Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs); 
(vi) Strengthening healthcare facilities upto District Hospital level so that patient 
need not be referred to tertiary hospitals;  

161 
 
(vii)  Strengthening infrastructure including Advanced Life Support (ALS) 
ambulances to handle cardiac cases and making available essential medicines and para-
medical staff at rural health centres as per the norms of the Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS) 2022 for strengthening/improving rural health infrastructure. Efforts 
should be made that all Health Schemes should be implemented at ground level 
especially in rural, semi-urban, tribal and hilly areas; 
(viii) Keeping in view the pivotal role of ASHA workers in the effective 
implementation of the various schemes of the Government on the ground level but being 
paid ranging from Rs. 5000- 9000 per month which is, of course, not sufficient for 
earning bread of two times for a single person, leave apart maintaining good health and 
basic needs, there is urgent need to enhance the honorarium of ASHA workers; 
(ix) Appreciating the decision of establishment of the Day Care Cancer Centres in all 
districts, particularly to provide the services to rural areas, in next three years, the 
Committee apprehends about the practical implementation of the provision on the 
ground level provided adequate budgetary allocation is made for the purpose. Although 
the Committee is uncertain about the Corporate Hospitals coming forward to join the 
programme, however, in case some Trust Hospitals come forward to participate in the 
programme, the Department should welcome the move and extend assistance & 
facilitate all kind of collaboration, co-operation and co-ordination network; 
(x) Keeping in view that the Department has formulated National Sickle Cell 
Anaemia Elimination Mission setting goal for screening of 7 crore population in the 
country. The Committee desires to know the number of population covered so far 
towards this goal and the number of persons given sickle cell genetic status card, along 
with the strategy chalked out to achieve the goal during 2026. The Committee wishes to 
highlight the incidence of sickle cell anaemia in tribal areas of the country, including 
Goa, where the Committee had recently visited and came across the prevalence of sickle 
cell anaemia in 1.5 lakh tribals, but without any certain provision for elimination of the 
disease. The Committee has further come across that even if ‘PSA’ Test Kit is available 
at the health centre, it is not opened till sufficient number of patients visit for full 
utilisation of the kit. The Committee is of the view that the health centre may be directed 
to open the ‘PSA’ Kit even if single patient visits the centre;  
(xi) Simplification of procedures/norms, rules and regulations for establishing 
nursing, occupational therapy & physiotherapy and dental colleges for ensuring their 
availability at the CHC and District Hospital level.  Arrangements be made for study of 
occupational therapy & physiotherapy in Government Hospital Colleges for producing 
sufficient number of occupational therapists and physiotherapists ensuring their 
services at the Block Level; and  
(xii) Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGMs) and diabetic medicines are essential for 
effective diabetes management which is a chronic disease condition. However, the high 
cost of CGMs, their limited lifespan and the lack of long-term insurance coverage for 
these devices and medicines create significant challenges for patients. The Committee, 

162 
 
therefore, recommends increasing the lifespan of CGM sensors, implementing price 
controls and price caps on CGM sensors, cardiac stents, etc., mandating insurance 
coverage for CGMs and diabetic medicines on a long term basis to ensure affordability 
and accessibility. The Committee further desires that ‘Make in India’ initiative should 
be promoted to reduce prices and achieve self-sufficiency in CGM production.

various levels in the Department of Health and Family Welfare which may impact the

5. The Committee acknowledges the increasing integration of technology in the 
health sector and emphasizes that modernizing healthcare services is essential for 
ensuring sustainable and affordable care. In this context, it is crucial for the workforce 
overseeing National health initiatives to actively engage with technological 
advancements. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare expand the use of technology and implement measures to strengthen 
the digital proficiency of its officials and staff. 
(Para 1.6.3) 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
6. The Department apprised the Committee that the budgetary allocation depends 
on the overall Government budgetary resources availability, the current demand by 
various Programme Divisions of the Department, availability of funds as per annual 
envelope of the schemes and pace of expenditure of the previous financial year. Ministry 
of Finance, accordingly, allocate ceiling of Budget Estimates. The Committee notes that 
a sum of Rs. 95,957.87 crore has been allocated to the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare for 2025-26, representing 1.89% of the total Union Budget estimate and 0.27% 
of GDP (at current prices). A review of past trends indicates that actual expenditure has 
often fallen short of the budgeted allocation, remaining at just 0.27% of GDP in both 
2022-23 and 2023-24. 
(Para 2.1.3) 
 
7. The Committee notes the 10.83% increase in the Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-
26 as compared to the Revised Estimate (RE) for 2024-25, but the Committee expresses 
concern over trend of the health sector's budget allocation, as a percentage of GDP and 
the total Union Budget that has been consistently declining since 2022-23. There is a 
need to accelerate the rate of improving healthcare to global standard and proportional 
to the rate of population growth. India being the most populous country, and given the 
inflationary pressures and the National Health Policy's target of increasing government 
health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025, the Committee believes that the allocation 
to the health sector, particularly to the Department of Health and Family Welfare, 
should have been much higher. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to take 
concrete steps to enhance the utilization of allocated funds effectively so that the targets 
set under a specific scheme are achieved. 
(Para 2.1.4) 

165 
 
BUDGETARY PROJECTION VIS-A-VIS ALLOCATION AND EXPENDITURE 
 
8. Over the past five years, it has been observed that the demand projected by the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare has been consistently low and has declined 
significantly compared to the 2021-22 level. Furthermore, budgetary allocations have 
continuously fallen short of the Department’s projected Demands for Grants, averaging 
a meager 0.3% of GDP at current prices. 
(Para 2.2.2) 
 
9. For the fiscal year 2025-26, the projected demand has increased to ₹1,00,702.79 
crore. However, given the inflation rate of 5.2% in December 2024, the population 
growth of the country and the National Health Policy’s goal of raising government 
health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025, the Committee believes that the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare must reassess its policy framework. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to request the Ministry of Finance 
for higher allocations for significantly enhancing healthcare infrastructure and 
healthcare services nationwide. This effort must be undertaken with urgency, 
particularly in light of the challenges faced during the COVID-19 pandemic, to ensure 
that the country is better prepared for the post-COVID era and for any future 
pandemics. 
(Para 2.2.3) 
 
10. The Committee notes that since FY 2022-23, the Revised Estimates have 
consistently been lower than the Budget Estimates. This trend undermines the 
credibility of the Department’s demand for higher fund allocations. Moreover, the 
concern is further reinforced by the fact that, except for FY 2023-24, the actual 
expenditure has remained below the Revised Estimate, which itself is already lower than 
the Budget Estimate. This raises concerns about the effective utilization of allocated 
funds in real terms. 
(Para 2.2.4) 
 
11. The Committee notes that, as of January 31, 2025, the Department had utilized 
81.32% of the total Revised Estimate, leaving 18.68% of the funds, approximately 
₹16,000 crores, available unspent for the remaining two months. The Ministry of 
Finance has repeatedly issued guidelines to regulate expenditure within a financial year. 
In its 143rd Report, the Committee recommended that the Department of Health and 
Family Welfare cap its expenditure in the final month of the financial year in 
accordance with existing guidelines and closely monitor fund utilization during the last 
quarter. This is crucial to ensuring the prudent and efficient use of allocated funds. 
(Para 2.2.5) 
 
12. Public health plays a crucial role in driving the country’s economic development. 
Given the inadequacy and overstretched nature of public health infrastructure, 
investments in the health sector must be increased. With inflation expected to remain 
high in the near term, the Department should consider for requesting higher budgetary 

166 
 
allocations for the health sector at the Revised Estimate stage and ensure the optimal 
utilization of allocated funds. 
(Para 2.2.6) 
 
13. The Committee notes that the primary determinant for revenue and capital 
outlay in healthcare budgeting is the annual, recurring demands from program divisions 
within the Department of Health & Family Welfare, coupled with the progress of 
ongoing projects. While the social service nature of the Department inherently limits 
capital expenditure, a recent push for infrastructure upgrades is evident, with "GIA-
Capital Creation" (grants-in-aid for capital creation) playing a significant role in 
boosting effective capital spending, despite being categorized under revenue. Analyzing 
the five-year trend reveals to the Committee that revenue expenditure consistently 
dominates, averaging over 90% of the total budget. However, the effective capital 
expenditure, including GIA-Capital, shows a fluctuating pattern in the period from FY 
2021-22 to FY 2025-26, decreasing consistently since the FY 2023-24, from 27.22 % in 
2022-23 to 15.60% in 2025-26 of the total allocation. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends establishing a formalized, multi-year strategic capital expenditure plan, 
distinct from annual recurring demands, that clearly outlines infrastructure 
development priorities and targets, including specific allocations for GIA-Capital, to 
ensure sustained and predictable growth in healthcare capital assets, thereby creating a 
more balanced approach between revenue and capital spending. 
(Para 2.2.8) 
 
GOVERNMENT HEALTH EXPENDITURE IN INDIA 
 
14. National Health Policy (NHP), 2017 prescribed increasing Government Health 
Expenditure (GHE) as a share of GDP to 2.5% by 2025. Following the objective of NHP, 
2017, GHE, as a share of GDP, has increased from 1.35% in 2017-18 to 1.84% in 2021-
22, indicating progress in health sector investment. The Committee notes that the 
upward trend in GHE is positive; however, further acceleration is required to meet the 
2.5% GDP target by 2025. The current pace of increase may not be sufficient to achieve 
this goal within the remaining timeframe. A strategic focus on public health 
infrastructure, preventive care, and efficient resource utilization will be crucial in 
ensuring long-term improvements in healthcare accessibility and quality. 
(Para 2.3.3) 
 
15. A close scrutiny of the Health Budget reflects the lack of priority assigned to 
health. The Committee observes that the declining trend in health budget allocation in 
terms of BE as % of GDP (at Current Price) between 2020-21 and 2024-25 (refer to 
Table 3 above) do not align with the target set in National Health Policy. The Committee 
is of the opinion that adequate health financing forms the pillar of a well-functioning 
health system which is crucial for reduction of Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) in 
health. The pandemic further reaffirmed the need of a sustainable health financing 
ecosystem especially in tackling a sudden public health crisis. The Committee 
recommends the Government to prioritize Health Sector in Budget Allocation by 

167 
 
increasing the annual budget allocation for healthcare to maintain the momentum and 
ensure sufficient resources for infrastructure, medical research, and service delivery. 
(Para 2.3.4) 
 
16. The Committee, in its 126th Report on DFG (2022-23), had also recommended the 
Government for increasing its health expenditure to 5% of GDP by 2025. However, with 
such stagnant allocation to health and the slow pace of increase in allocation, the goal of 
achieving the NHP target of health expenditure to 2.5% seems a distant dream.  
(Para 2.3.5) 
 
17. The Committee is of the view that strengthening of public health infrastructure,  
enhancing preventive and primary care services, leveraging Public-Private Partnerships 
(PPP), exploring additional revenue sources, innovation in health, robust monitoring 
and evaluation mechanism to track the utilization of health funds and assess the impact 
are crucial for establishing an affordable and accessible healthcare delivery system, 
especially for a developing economy like India. The need of the hour is to recognize 
health as a key sector for economic as well as social development. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends the Government to make health a priority and increase 
its investment in the health sector.  
(Para 2.3.6) 
 
18. The Committee acknowledges that various Government schemes have 
progressively expanded the scope of social security and broadened the list of 
beneficiaries. This sustained intervention has contributed to a notable decline in Out-of-
Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) on healthcare, which has reduced from 48.8% in 2017-18 
to 39.4% in 2021-22. The Committee is quite optimistic that the current figures for 
OOPE might be lower than 39.4. However, the Committee apprehends that 39.4% 
OOPE out of THE continues to be a significant barrier to accessing quality healthcare. 
As per the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2024, India is home to approximately 
234 million poor people, the highest in the world. Also, in the five countries with the 
largest number of people living in poverty, India is the only country with medium 
Human Development Index (HDI) and the remaining four are low HDI. Given this large 
population deprived of basic amenities, increased Government health spending is crucial 
to ensuring affordable healthcare access.  
(Para 2.3.10) 
 
19. The Committee observes that GHE as % of GDP of India (1.84%) is very low 
when compared to the developed countries like USA, UK, Japan and Germany. Hence, 
there is ample inspiration for the Government to make sustained efforts to increase the 
GHE which would have the declining effects on OOPE. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Government intensify efforts to increase GHE and further reduce 
OOPE. The Committee urges the Government to adopt best practices from High-
Income Countries (HICs), where nearly 70% of healthcare expenditure is publicly 
funded, and ensuring greater financial protection for citizens. 
(Para 2.3.11) 

168 
 
 
20. The Committee understands that increasing the public investment on health 
depends on several factors such as State Government’s health budget depending on their 
allocations, capacities and fund position, transfer to states on the recommendation on 
Finance Commission, allocation made under Centrally Sponsored Schemes by Union 
Government based on total budgetary resources. The Committee appreciates that the 25 
States and the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry as per the NHA Estimates for 
FY 2021-22 have achieved the National Health Policy target of 8% of their budget 
allocated to health. The Committee recommends that other State/UT Governments 
should follow the same. 
(Para 2.3.13) 
 
21. The Committee, in its 134th Report, had highlighted the existing wide inter-State 
and intra-State disparity in healthcare infrastructure across the country. The 
Committee observes that States with poor financial resources and inefficient fiscal 
capacity face umpteen challenges in establishing a robust health infrastructure. The 
Committee, accordingly, reiterates its recommendation that the Union Government 
must persuade the remaining State/UT Governments to achieve the prescribed 
budgetary health expenditure to 8% of State General Government Expenditure. 
(Para 2.3.14) 
 
22. The Committee observes that the data on General Health Expenditure (GHE), 
Total Health Expenditure (THE), Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE), and other 
relevant indicators is only available up to the year 2021-22, with the National Health 
Accounts (NHA) Estimates for 2021-22 being released in September 2024. The 
Committee expresses concern over delay in updating data as old and obsolete data 
significantly hampers the assessment of the progress made by various government 
schemes and policies. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to 
update data pertaining to GHE, THE, OOPE, etc. without delay, sooner the better.  
(Para 2.3.15) 
 
23. In today's digital age, where Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence 
play a key role, it is crucial to leverage these tools for the efficient collection and real-
time processing of data. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Government 
take immediate steps to integrate digital tools into the data collection process. 
Additionally, the Government should ensure that data for a given financial year is made 
available by the last quarter of the following financial year. This approach will 
rationalize data analysis, enabling more effective evaluation and improvement of 
government schemes and policies, ensuring they are aligned with the intended objectives 
and targeted effectively. 
(Para 2.3.16) 
15th FINANCE COMMISSION HEALTH GRANTS 
 
24. The Committee observes that, as of January 30, 2025, only 39.42% of the funds 
approved by the 15th Finance Commission for the States have been released, with only 

169 
 
the funds for the fiscal year 2021-22 being fully disbursed. The States have reported 
spending only 59.31% of the released funds. These funds were specifically allocated to 
address gaps in primary healthcare facilities across the country. However, the States' 
low utilization of these funds undermines the purpose of this financial support. In light 
of these concerns, the Committee strongly recommends that the Government conduct a 
comprehensive study to determine the underlying causes of this under-utilization and 
implement measures to resolve these issues. Furthermore, the Union Government should 
establish a dedicated communication channel with the States to facilitate continuous

CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS):  
 
25. The Committee acknowledges the Government's efforts to digitize healthcare 
resources through the Healthcare Management Information System (HMIS), establish 
new Wellness Centres in tier-II cities, and promote Ayush Centres. However, the 
examination of budget allocation and utilization under Revenue Head reflects a 
significant gap between the RE allocation of Rs. 2245.82 crore for CGHS and the actual 
expenditure of Rs. 1842.51 crore, representing only 82% utilization as of February 7, 
2025. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department conducts a thorough 
and immediate review of the CGHS expenditure process, specifically focusing on 
identifying and addressing the bottlenecks causing the underutilization of allocated 
funds. By streamlining administrative procedures, improving procurement processes, 
and ensuring timely disbursement of funds, the Department can ensure that the 
allocated resources are effectively used to enhance healthcare services for beneficiaries, 
thereby maintaining the intended continuity between budget allocation and service 
delivery. 
(Para 3.1.4) 
 
26. In its 155th Report, the Committee observed that, as of August 2023, 26% of the 
340 allopathic wellness centres (spread across 80 cities) were concentrated in the Delhi 
NCR region. Additionally, only six states (excluding Delhi NCR) have more than ten 
CGHS centres, while Arunachal Pradesh and the Union Territories of Ladakh, 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep have none. The Committee noted that 
CGHS services are unevenly distributed, limiting accessibility in many regions. The 
Committee, therefore, wishes to highlight that numerous cities and towns with a 
significant population of Central Government employees, pensioners, and their 
dependents lack CGHS wellness centres. As a result, beneficiaries—particularly 
retirees—have to travel long distances for medical treatment, causing financial strain 
and other hardships. To address this, the Committee urges the Ministry to proactively 
advocate for new CGHS centres in underserved areas, particularly in suburban regions 
with a substantial number of serving and retired beneficiaries. The Committee 

170 
 
recommends that the Ministry engage with the Ministry of Finance for speedy approval 
of new CGHS Wellness Centres. Moreover, the Committee suggests that the 
Government should consider revising existing norms or introducing new ones to

that it can be achieved through: (i) intensified training and capacity building for 
healthcare workers at all levels on IHIP data entry & analytics and utilization; (ii) 
streamlined data entry processes and user interface improvements to minimize 
reporting burdens; (iii) regular monitoring and feedback mechanisms to identify and 
rectify reporting challenges; and (iv) leveraging the recently launched community 
reporting tool to supplement and validate data from health facilities, thereby fostering a 
more comprehensive and robust surveillance system. 
(Para 3.10.12) 
 
70. The Committee recommends building on existing collaborations with NACP and 
NFHS, it should implement a standardized framework for data collection and scientific 
analysis of data, integrating seroprevalence data across multiple disease areas to ensure 
continuity and clarity between surveillance of data and programmatic action. This 
expansion will optimize laboratory infrastructure, generate a comprehensive dataset 
essential for informed policymaking, targeted interventions, and effective disease 
control. 
(Para 3.10.14)

71. The Committee has been apprised of the indigenously developed Adverse Drug 
Reaction Monitoring Software (ADRMS) of Pharmacovigilance Program of India 
(PvPI) launched on 19th August 2024. The Committee recommends a strategic focus on 
improving the functionality and accessibility of this indigenously developed ADRM 
software to strengthen the efficacy and safety database for new drugs. The key measures 
in this direction should include implementing rigorous data validation and quality 
control protocols; expanding targeted training programs and developing user-friendly 
interfaces and advanced data analytics tools within ADRMS to enable timely signal 
detection and benefit-risk analysis, reinforcing the program’s leadership in international 
drug monitoring and safeguarding public health. The whole purpose is to create 
effective nation-wide system for patient safety reporting in respect to adverse drug 
reactions (ADRs) of medical products. 
(Para 3.11.4)

72. The Committee believes that, to achieve sustained improvements in nursing 
services and rectify geographical disparities, the Government need to implement a 
comprehensive, data-driven strategy for the targeted expansion and enhancement of 
nursing education and training with a particular focus on underserved regions. The 
Committee urges for integrated implementation of the existing Central Sector Scheme 
for the Development of Nursing Services, the establishment of 157 new nursing colleges 
in co-location with existing medical colleges, and the Continuing Nursing Education 
(CNE) framework. The Committee further recommends that the scheme must 
emphasize the training of nurses in the field of specialization, frequent/periodic in-

183 
 
service training, infrastructure development by way of strengthening of Schools and 
upgrading of Schools of Nursing to Colleges of Nursing. 
(Para 3.12.6) 
 
73. The Committee is of the opinion that Government should actively enforce CNE 
regulations with rigorous monitoring of training outcomes to ensure that all nurses 
maintain their competency through mandatory training. The approval and funding 
processes for state government proposals should be streamlined, expediting 
infrastructure development and training initiatives. These measures will directly 
address the shortage of qualified nursing personnel and enhance healthcare delivery 
across India. Additionally, the Committee give emphasis to the efficient utilization of 
allocated funds and the strategic distribution of resources based on state-wise data on 
nursing institutions and admission capacities. 
(Para 3.12.7) 
 
HEALTH SECTOR DISASTER PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE AND HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT FOR EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES 
 
74.    The Committee noted the under-utilisation of funds under Health Sector Disaster 
Preparedness and Response and Human Resource Development for Emergency Medical 
Services during the past two years. In the FY 2023-24, Rs. 128.14 crore was allocated at 
BE stage which was reduced to Rs. 70 crore at RE stage. Moreover, the actual 
expenditure was just Rs. 30.50 crore (43.57% of the already reduced revised estimate). 
Similarly, in the next FY 2024-25, the amount of Rs. 94 crore allocated at BE stage was 
reduced to Rs. 15 crore at RE stage, and again, the actual expenditure has been reported 
to the tune of Rs. 7.57 crore as on 07.02.2025. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Government to implement a rigorous, time-bound monitoring and evaluation 
framework for the "Health Sector Disaster Preparedness and Response and Human 
Resource Development for Emergency Medical Services" scheme, specifically focusing 
on the timely execution of infrastructure projects and Capacity Building Initiatives that 
inter-alia include setting up of National Emergency Life Support (NELS) skill centers in 
medical colleges/institutions under Central/State Government and setting up of 
Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) medical management centers 
besides imparting skills training of doctors, nurses and paramedics on NELS and 
CBRN, and fund utilization by grantee institutions. 
(Para 3.13.6) 
 
75.     For efficient and optimal utilization of funds under the scheme, the Committee 
believes that the Government should consider the following: (i) pre-identified and vetted 
site alternatives to mitigate delays due to site changes; (ii) mandatory quarterly fund 
utilization reports from grantee medical colleges for NELS Skill Centers, with clear 
timelines for disbursement and penalties for non-compliance; and (iii) a proactive, 
needs-based assessment system for disaster and public health emergency response 
logistics, rather than solely relying on state/UT requests, to ensure allocated funds are 

184 
 
strategically utilized. This systematic approach will address the recurrent issues of 
delayed project execution and underutilization of funds. 
(Para 3.13.7)

76. The Committee notes that the funds utilization trend under the National Organ 
Transplant Program (NOTP) show significant discrepancies between budgeted and 
actual expenditures, indicating poor fund utilization. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Government to establish a robust mechanism incorporating 
accountability and ensuring enhanced and effective fund utilization by ROTTOs and 
SOTTOs. The Department needs to address the root causes of underutilization, 
including administrative bottlenecks and lack of state-level capacity and overcome the 
reasons for under-utilization and also persuading the non-performing States for optimal 
utilization of allocated fund.  
(Para 3.14.5) 
 
77. The Committee, on examination of the submissions made by the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare, observes that many ROTTOs and SOTTOs are in their 
infancy stage, lacking infrastructure and operational efficiency. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the strengthening of ROTTOs and SOTTOs by provide 
comprehensive capacity-building programs for ROTTOs and SOTTOs, focusing on 
website development, data management, budget utilization, and training program 
organization. 
(Para 3.14.6) 
NATIONAL TELE MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME 
 
78. The Committee notes significant under-utilisation of fund under the National 
Tele Mental Health Programme. In both FYs 2023-24 and 2024-25, the allocation of 
funds at RE stage was significantly reduced as compared to the allocation at BE stage. 
The Committee believes in immediate and targeted interventions to resolve bottlenecks 
in fund utilization to ensure the sustained growth and effectiveness of Tele MANAS. 
Further, the recruitment processes for human resources at the State and Union 
Territory levels must be expedited through streamlined procedures and proactive 
central government support.  
(Para 3.15.3) 
 
79. The Committee urges upon the Department for an intensified focus on targeted 
outreach and awareness campaigns to build on the increasing engagement of female 
callers and extend services to vulnerable populations. These efforts should leverage the 
Tele MANAS mobile application and diverse media platforms to address specific 
barriers preventing access to services. Furthermore, the nationwide expansion of video 
consultation services, currently available in select states, should be prioritized to 
enhance accessibility, particularly for individuals in remote and underserved areas. This 
expansion must be supported by comprehensive training and technical assistance to 

185 
 
ensure effective implementation and utilization of the video consultation platform. 
 
(Para 3.15.4) 
 
NATIONAL DIGITAL HEALTH MISSION (NDHM)/ AYUSHMAN BHARAT 
DIGITAL MISSION (ABDM) 
 
80. The Committee, on examination of the Demands for Grants (2025-26), observes 
with concern persistent and declining trend of utilisation of funds allocated under the 
ABDM. In the FY 2023-24, in BE an amount of Rs. 341.02 crore was allocated to the 
scheme which was reduced to Rs. 200 crore at RE stage and at the end of the FY, the 
actual expenditure came to Rs. 175.36 crore (just 51.42% of BE allocated initially). In 
FY 2024-25, the BE allocation was reduced to Rs. 200 crore (which is a reduction by 
41.35% from the BE 2023-24), however, at RE stage the allocation was increased to Rs. 
225 crore, but the actual expenditure up to 31.01.2025 comes to Rs. 112.97 crore only 
(which is just 50.21% of the RE allocation).  This pattern of under-expenditure, coupled 
with fluctuating budget allocations, directly hampers the scheme's ability to achieve its 
targeted objectives within the stipulated timeframe, potentially leading to time delays 
and cost overruns. To rectify this situation, the Committee recommends immediate and 
decisive action to address the root causes of these inefficiencies and streamline the fund 
utilization for successful implementation of Mission. In the FY 2025-26, the scheme has 
been allocated an enhanced amount of Rs. 340.11 crore at BE stage. The Committee, 
therefore, urges upon the Department to address the issues with strategic planning and 
project execution to ensure proper utilization of the funds so that intended targets are 
achieved within stipulated time-frame.  
(Para 3.16.5) 
 
81. Given the recurring issues of underutilization of funds within the Ayushman 
Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), specifically due to delays in state-level Project 
Monitoring Unit (PMU) establishment, inefficient management of advertising contracts, 
performance issues with Managed Service Providers (MSPs), and complications in 
professional service contracts, the Committee recommends a robust fund disbursement 
and monitoring mechanism should be instituted. This should include strict timelines and 
performance-linked incentives for States/UTs to expedite the establishment of Project 
Monitoring Units (PMUs), along with real-time tracking of fund allocation and 
utilization. Furthermore, ensuring timely on-boarding of competent service providers 
and enforcing clear contractual obligations with penalties for non-performance will help 
streamline expenditure under Digital Equipment and Professional Services. 
Strengthening coordination between NHA, States/UTs, and implementing agencies will 
be critical for optimizing fund flow and ensuring effective implementation of ABDM 
objectives. 
(Para 3.16.7) 
 
82. The Committee recommends to fully leveraging the potential of AI and ML in 
healthcare by accelerating the integration and scaling of AI-driven tools within the 

186 
 
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM). Specifically, the successful collaborations, 
such as the MoU with IIT Kanpur and the AI-based Clinical Decision Support System 
(CDSS) in e-Sanjeevani, should be rapidly replicated. This includes prioritizing the 
development and deployment of unified learning platforms, quality-preserving 
databases, and open benchmarking systems, ensuring that these technologies are 
accessible and beneficial across all healthcare facilities, especially in rural and 
underserved areas. This will enhance diagnostic accuracy, streamline patient care, and 
improve overall health outcomes by making data-driven decisions more efficient. 
(Para 3.16.10) 
 
83. The Committee believes that the ABDM should effectively reach rural and tribal 
populations for gains in real terms. The Committee, in this connection, emphasizes the 
need for enhanced digital literacy and connectivity initiatives alongside the mission's 
technical advancements. The NHA should intensify efforts to implement and promote 
the assisted mode for ABHA creation in areas with poor internet connectivity and 
limited digital literacy. Additionally, targeted awareness campaigns and training 
programs should be conducted in local languages to educate healthcare providers and 
citizens about the benefits and usage of ABDM services like Scan and Share and Scan 
and Pay. Collaborations with local community leaders and NGOs can further facilitate 
the adoption of ABDM, ensuring that even the most remote populations have equitable 
access to digital health services while maintaining robust privacy and security measures. 
(Para 3.16.11) 
 
STATUTORY AND REGULATORY BODIES 
 
84. The Committee notes that the reduction in budgetary allocation for the Food 
Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) in the RE 2024-25 was primarily due 
to delayed submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs) from States/UTs. This delay 
hinders the timely disbursement of funds for strengthening the food safety ecosystem. 
The committee, therefore, recommends the Department for implementing a streamlined 
UC submission and tracking system. To ensure consistent and timely fund utilization, 
the FSSAI should establish a mandatory, digitally enabled system for States/UTs to 
submit and track their UCs. This system should include automated reminders and alerts 
for pending submissions, and provide real-time visibility of UC status to both FSSAI and 
the respective States/UTs. Furthermore, the FSSAI should conduct periodic workshops 
and training sessions for State/UT officials to improve their understanding of UC 
requirements and submission processes, thereby preventing future delays and ensuring 
efficient fund utilization. This proactive approach will facilitate smoother fund flow and 
enable FSSAI to effectively carry out its mandate of ensuring food safety across the 
country. 
(Para 3.17.6) 
 
85. Given the importance of FSSAI's activities, particularly in supporting 
States/UTs, the Committee is of the opinion that a phased funding release tied to 
performance and capacity building should be implemented. Instead of a single annual 

187 
 
allocation, funds could be released in tranches, contingent upon the timely submission of 
UCs and demonstrable progress in enhancing food safety infrastructure and 
surveillance. In addition, a portion of the funds should be dedicated to capacity-building 
initiatives, such as training programs for food safety officers, procurement of essential 
equipment, and the establishment of robust laboratory facilities at the state and local 
levels. This approach will incentivize States/UTs to prioritize food safety initiatives, 
improve their administrative efficiency, and build sustainable food safety systems. 
                (Para 3.17.7) 
 
86. The Committee notes that FSSAI is actively deploying Mobile Food Testing 
Laboratories (MFTLs) to enhance on-the-spot food testing and awareness, and while 
progress is made in this connection, achieving the target of one MFTL/FSW per district 
by 2026 is contingent on state readiness. The Committee recommends FSSAI to 
implement a structured program to actively assist states in achieving 
readiness/willingness to deploy MFTLs/FSWs. The Committee feels that through 
dedicated State liaisons, FSSAI personnel should work directly with state governments 
to identify and address specific barriers to FSW deployment. The Committee desires 
that targeted training programs and expedited funding mechanisms should be 
established showing proactive approach to prevent delays and ensure consistent food 
safety monitoring across all districts. 
(Para 3.17.13) 
 
87. FSSAI faces a significant number of vacant positions, which could impact its 
operational efficiency. The Committee believes that to improve the operational 
efficiency of FSSAI and enhance the consistency of food safety regulation across the 
country, FSSAI should be directed to prioritize and expedite the direct recruitment 
process to fill up the significant number of vacant positions. Additionally, FSSAI should 
implement strategies to improve employee retention and recruitment on regular basis 
must be adhered to instead of hiring staff on contract basis as contractual staff lacks 
sense of organizational belongingness and commitment to work and there remain sense 
of being on ad-hoc at work that too without responsibility and accountability. The 
Committee, therefore, believes that efforts be made to grant regularization of 
contractual staff in FSSAI.  
(Para 3.17.14) 
 
88. Furthermore, the Committee notes that not all States have separate food safety 
departments, which could lead to inconsistencies in implementation, however, most of 
the States have Food Safety Appellate Tribunals.  The Committee, therefore, holds that 
separate Food Safety Departments should be promoted. The Committee strongly 
emphasizes the Department to encourage the remaining states/UTs to establish separate 
Food Safety Departments. Providing guidance and examples of the benefits of separate 
departments, as well as possible assistance during the transition, will help to increase the 
number of states with separate departments. 
(Para 3.17.15)

projects is not satisfactory, which can be corroborated by the fact that out of the six

projects. The key issues include delayed Project implementation, weak project planning 
and execution, delay in tendering process and environmental and regulatory hurdles.

monitoring mechanism with clearly defined milestones and regular progress reviews.

hurdles, such as environmental clearances and tree-cutting approvals, by engaging with 
relevant authorities at the earliest stages of project planning. Furthermore, AIIMS 
should streamline its tendering process to minimize/eliminate delays, potentially through

redevelopment project, given the project's extremely slow progress (2.50% physical,

to this project, and its efficient utilization.

("Ashray"), enhancing patient convenience through various facilities, streamlining

appointments via online systems, expanding infrastructure with new specialty blocks,

at transforming it into a world-class medical university, is progressing but faces delays 
due to land acquisition and budgetary approvals. Simultaneously, the Department must 
expedite the approval and allocation of the necessary budgetary resources for the 
AIIMS Master Plan. To ensure timely execution, a dedicated project management team 
should be established to oversee the phased implementation of the plan, with regular 
progress reviews and reporting to the Committee. This will ensure that the 
infrastructure upgrades are completed without further delay, and that AIIMS can reach 
its goal to become a world class medical university. 
(Para 3.18.10)

the Sr. Resident (Non-Academic) posts have 434 vacancies (37.48% of the sanctioned 
strength) and Jr. Resident (Non-Academic) have 113 vacancies (46.89% of the 
sanctioned strength). In addition to the above, the Department has submitted that there

work flow. Given the substantial number of vacant regular staff positions, the

mobilize additional resources, ensure close coordination with local authorities to address

logistical and security concerns, and leverage technology for real-time tracking of

particularly in Group A category. Moreover, there exist substantial vacancies of the post 
of Senior Residents (Contractual position). The Committee has also been apprised of the

proposals for pay scale upgrades and the creation/revival of essential posts. Addressing 
the critical vacancies, particularly in Group A positions and Senior Resident roles, is
