1 
 
CHAPTER- I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Medical Colleges and Seats in India 
 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee notes that the current situation regarding medical seats both in UG and PG 
in our country is a critical issue that warrants immediate attention. With an annual influx of 
approximately 2 million aspiring medical students at UG and only 1/20ti mes available seats, the 
demand far exceeds the supply, similarly, the number of available seats at PG level is far less 
than the demand. The Committee acknowledges the urgency of addressing this challenge while 
maintaining the quality of medical education  at its highest standard. To address this issue 
effectively, several measures can be taken. First and foremost, there is a need to significantly 
increase medical seats in both undergraduate and postgraduate courses. The government's 
existing scheme, which focuses on the establishment of new medical colleges attached to district 
or referral hospitals, can be instrumental in achieving this goal. By expanding this initiative, the 
Government can create more opportunities for aspiring medical students.  
(Para 2.4 of the Report) 
 
1.1.2 The Committee further recommends that it is essential to make optimal use of the existing 
infrastructure. Ensuring that all available resources and facilities are utilized efficiently can help 
accommodate a larger number of students without compromising t he quality of education. 
Additionally, streamlining the admission process by implementing a standardized national 
entrance examination can improve fairness and transparency in seat allocation.  
(Para 2.5 of the Report) 
 
1.1.3 Encouraging private investment  in medical education is another avenue to explore. 
Providing incentives and regulatory support to private institutions willing to establish medical 
colleges can not only increase seat availability but also introduce healthy competition and 
innovation in m edical education. The Committee also recommends the Ministry leverage 
technology for distance learning and organise virtual classrooms that can be a supplementary 
solution to address the shortage of seats, allowing a more significant number of students to access 
medical education without overburdening physical infrastructure.  
(Para 2.6 of the Report) 
 
 

2 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.4 There are 706 medical colleges that admit close to 110,000 medical students each year for 
MBBS course. Close to 70,000 seats are available for postgraduate education under NMC 
recognized institutions as well as the NBEMS recognized hospitals. 
 
The government has launched new post -graduate courses in emerging and in -demand specialties 
such as Geriatric Medicine, Emergency Medicine, S ports Medicine, Palliative Medicine, and 
Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. This initiative seeks to address the shortage of specialists in 
these vital areas while expanding the availability of PG seats in medical colleges. To ensure that 
vacant seats are filled after the counseling process, the admission benchmark percentile has been 
reduced. However, the cut -off marks will not fall below a set minimum to maintain the high 
standards of medical education in the country. 
The Guidelines for Undergraduate Cou rses, as outlined in the Establishment of New Medical 
Institutions, Starting of New Medical Courses, Increase of Seats for Existing Courses & 
Assessment and Rating Regulations 2023 (MSR -2023), specify the minimum infrastructure and 
faculty requirements based on student intake. Any relaxation in these requirements would require 
a policy revision of MSR-2023. According to these guidelines, a 50 -seat UG medical college can 
be established if a fully functional hospital with 220 beds is available. 
The quality of  medical education is determined by three key factors: clinical material 
(authenticated by ABHA ID), trained faculty (confirmed through AEBAS), and infrastructure 
(verified through inspections, including virtual ones). The NMC has updated requirements per 
student admission and reduced the number of mandatory departments. Consultations with 
stakeholders suggest a student limit of 150 per class to improve fairness and overall quality. 
Priority is given to opening colleges in underserved areas, which will impr ove healthcare 
accessibility through better hospitals.  
NEET-UG, NEET-PG, and NEET -SS are the entrance exams conducted for medical admissions 
at various level such as MBBS/PG courses/SS courses. The counseling process for each exam is 
centralized or state -specific, where seats are allocated based on ranks, reservation policies, and 
institutional preferences which ensures a standardized and transparent admission process.  
As of the academic year 2025 -26, over 300 private, society, and trust -run medical colle ges are 
recognized by the NMC. Under current regulations, any private entity can establish a medical 
college by meeting the requirements set forth in MSR-2023.  
The government has increased number of medical colleges and subsequently increased MBBS 
seats. There is an increase of 102% in Medical Colleges from 387 before 2014 to 780 as of now. 
Further, there is an increase of 130% in MBBS seats from 51,348 before 2014 to 1,18,190 as of 
now and increase of 138.3% in PG seats from 31,185 before 2014 to 74,306 a s of now. 
Furthermore, there is an increase of 69.4% in Private medical colleges from 206 before 2014 to 
349 as of now whereas total increase of 114.8% UG seats in private medical colleges from 26880 
before 2014 to 57766 as of now. 
 

3 
 
1.1.5 The measures/steps taken by the Government to increase the doctor/medical professional in 
the country include:- 
i. Centrally Sponsored Scheme for establishment of new medical college by upgrading 
district/ referral hospital under which 131 new medical colleges are already fun ctional 
out of 157 approved medical colleges.  
ii. Centrally Sponsored Scheme for strengthening/ upgradation of existing State 
Government/Central Government Medical Colleges to increase MBBS and PG seats. 
iii. Under “Upgradation of Government Medical Colleges by co nstruction of Super 
Specialty Blocks” of Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) scheme, a 
total of 75 projects have been approved, of which 69 projects are complete.    
iv. Under the Central Sector Scheme for setting up of new AIIMS, 22 AIIMS have bee n 
approved. Undergraduate courses have started in 19 of these. 
v. DNB qualification has been recognized for appointment as faculty to take care of 
shortage of faculty. 
vi. Enhancement of age limit for appointment/ extension/ re -employment against posts of 
teachers/Dean/Principal/ Director in medical colleges upto 70 years. 
 
The latest NMC regulations have simplified the process of establishing new institutions, making 
it easier to start medical colleges. A 220-bed hospital, for example, can support a medical college, 
and initiating PG education in such hospitals demands significantly lower infrastructure costs. 
 
Imbalance in Distribution of Medical Colleges 
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The WHO norms recommend a doctor -population ratio of 1:1000, and as per the NMC, the 
country has already achieved a ratio of 1:856. However, the concern area associated with opening 
a new medical college is the number of prescribed department -wise and total patient Bed 
capacity, read along with the requirement of their 80 per cent average occupancy in the attached 
hospital. The Committee would recommend the Government that such one - size-fits-all criterion 
prescribed in the UG -MSR may be revisited to take into account the geographic imbalances, if 
any, and formulate region-specific guidelines/ norms.  
(Para 2.12 of the Report) 
 
1.2.2 The Committee also recommends the Government to chalk out a comprehensive India -
specific approach that considers the nation's healthcare needs in the next 20 -25 years, identifies 
the categories of doctors, viz. pediatricians, ophthalmologists, neurosurg eons, critical care 
specialists, infectious disease specialists that the country would need rather than just randomly 

4 
 
increasing general surgery, pharma, and anatomy seats. The Committee believes that such a 
concerted effort to produce need -based specialis ts/ doctors commensurate with disease -burden 
specialists will secure India's healthcare needs in the future. The Committee recommends that in 
the case of the current scenario modalities for a fair distribution of doctors„ workforce across the 
country espec ially in underprivileged areas can be worked out by the NMC by offering 
incentives, monetary or otherwise.  
(Para 2.13 of the Report) 
 
1.2.3 The Committee notes that a travel time of 30 minutes between the college campus and the 
attached hospital has been prescribed in the guidelines. The Committee while taking cognisance 
of the rationale behind this travel time criteria fails to understand the logic behind keeping 
separate distance criteria of 30 kilometers (Tier -I cities) and 50 kilometers (for other cities) 
between RHTC/UHTC/CHC and the medical college. The Committee recommends the National 
Medical Commission review this criterion and cons ider incorporating suitable travel time instead 
of distance.  
(Para 2.14 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.2.4 It is desirable to cross WHO standards, particularly when comparing the doctor -to-public 
ratio with that of developed countries. Government is utilizing available hospitals to enhance 
medical education, with the NMC playing an active role in supporting this initiative. A 
significant step forward is the revision of teacher eligibility qualifications, allowing existing 
specialists to be appointed o r re -designated as faculty members. The requirement for three 
mandated departments for starting an MBBS course has been removed, and colleges now receive 
recognition status from the outset, rather than after five years. Annual declarations by colleges, as 
mandated in the Act, will be evaluated, and renewals based on these reports will facilitate 
permission for annual admissions. 
 
1.2.5 To optimize the use of available resources, the Minimum Standard Requirements for 
Postgraduate Courses 2024 (PGMSR -2024) ha ve been updated. These reforms facilitate the 
introduction of PG courses with two seats, standalone PG courses in government hospitals, and 
the simultaneous introduction of PG courses alongside UG courses in government colleges. 
Additionally, the required number of beds per unit for starting PG courses has been reduced, and 
it is no longer mandatory to have a Senior Resident for the initial two seats, which will help 
increase postgraduate admissions. 
1.2.6 Strengthening the quality of medical education is a lso a priority, addressed through reforms 
in regulations, MSR requirements, curriculum updates, and changes to assessment methods.  
1.2.7 There is an urgent need to standardize the number of specialists in each medical field. 
Planning for the required numb er of specialists over the next decades is critical, and multiple 
inputs are necessary to forecast these figures. PGMER -2023 aligns with the NMC‟s mandate to 
address specialized healthcare needs through structured training for super-specialty courses under 
the NEET-SS exam. It also includes a District Residency Program to support capacity expansion 
in critical areas. 

5 
 
1.2.8 As per MSR -2023, Schedule -I, the college must be situated on a single plot, with the 
distance between the college and hospital not excee ding a 30 -minute travel time, ensuring 
efficient use of students' time. Additionally, for internship training, as outlined in MSR -2023, 
Schedule-I, clause 6.5(a), interns in X category (Tier -1) cities may be posted to Health Centers 
within 30 km, with the limit extended to 50 km in rural or hard -to-reach areas due to 
transportation challenges. 
 
Evaluation of the existing curriculum and its relevance to healthcare needs, the need for 
transformation 
 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee notes that the NMC guidelines on Competency -Based Medical Education 
(CBME) Regulations, 2023, are comprehensive and comparable to best global practices and thus 
a welcome step in upgrading the curriculum of medical education in India. The Committee, 
however, believes there are some areas where the guidelines could be improved to make them 
more feasible and effective in the Indian context. The current policies need to be more 
transparent in implementing CBME in practice. Implementing CBME ca n be challenging for 
medical colleges, especially those with limited resources. Specific guidance to develop the 
CBME curricula, assessments, and teaching methods would prove to be useful in reaping early 
benefits. Furthermore, the Committee feels that the  transition to CBME will require significant 
changes to medical education programs; therefore, medical colleges will need support, including 
augmenting faculty training and access to resources from the NMC and other stakeholders in 
making this transition. The Committee also notes that medical colleges in India vary widely 
regarding resources, faculty expertise, and student demographics. The CBME guidelines should 
consider this diversity and be flexible enough to be implemented in different settings. The CBME 
guidelines should consider this diversity and be flexible enough to be implemented in different 
settings. To maintain the true spirit of CBME, the Committee feels that there should be a regular 
periodic review and monitoring of the medical curriculum.  
(Para 2.16 of the report) 
 
1.3.2 The Committee acknowledges the critical elements introduced in the new curriculum to 
help students acquire practical skills. The Committee strongly recommends the rigorous and 
comprehensive implementation of the AETCOM module within the MBBS curriculum.  This 
module is paramount as it is pivotal in cultivating the right attitude, ethics, and communication 
skills among medical students. Patient care is not solely about clinical knowledge and technical 
skills; it hinges on empathy, compassion, and effective  communication. By instilling these 
qualities in future healthcare professionals, we can significantly enhance the overall quality of 
patient care. Therefore, the Committee recommends the Government ensure that the AETCOM 
module is enforced consistently an d effectively to empower medical students with the essential 
attributes needed to provide holistic and patient - centered healthcare. In addition to the 
implementation of AETCOM, the Committee recommends the incorporation of these criteria in 

6 
 
NEET so that the aptitude of aspiring medical students can be assessed. Such aptitude tests at the 
entrance level go beyond mere knowledge assessment of aspirants, often obtained through rote 
learning and mastering MCQ -based exams, and evaluate the genuine interest and passion of the 
candidate for the field of medicine. It will enable the system to identify candidates who have a 
sincere calling for the profession and distinguish them from those who may be under external 
pressure or legacy expectations. By doing so, we ca n ensure that medical work continues to 
attract individuals who are genuinely committed to delivering high-quality healthcare.  
(Para 2.18 of the report) 
 
 
1.3.3 In a general context, the Committee has observed that there is a frequent change in the 
regulations notified by the National Medical Commission. The Committee would recommend 
that before notification of any regulation, a robust and thorough study involving the opinions/ 
viewpoints of various stakeholders should be undertaken. 
(Para 2.19 of the report) 
 
1.3.4 The Committee was apprised of the fact that some private medical colleges seemingly fail 
medical graduates deliberately during mid -semester exams which results in repetition of the 
semester, and charging additional fees for repeating the semester or exa m. This practice causes 
stress on the medical students, financial and otherwise. The Committee therefore recommends 
that UGMEB may develop appropriate feasible modalities for monitoring assessment, 
revaluation, etc. without charging any additional fee.  
(Para 2.20 of the report) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.3.5 The curriculum for the undergraduate medical education has been revised with a focus on 
skill building. The competence based medical education is a refined  way of imparting those 
skills. This is also facilitated by early clinical exposure to these students. Focus has been shifted 
to both vertical and horiz ontal integration of training. Training in soft skills, such as attitude, 
ethics, and communication is emphasised at all levels of their education us ing the module that is 
separately developed for this purpose. Students are encouraged to get an exposure in Ayush 
systems as electives in the student as well as in the internship days. Students are given an option 
to accumulate extra credit points in diffe rent areas that are not necessa rily covered in the 
curriculum. The postgraduate education has prescribed some minimum inputs by way of various 
clinical procedures in different select specialties. 
 
1.3.6 Guidelines on Competency -Based Medical Education (CBME) Regulations, 2023, have 
been reviewed by the Undergraduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB) to enhance the quality 
of medical education in India. This review has led to the issuance of the new CBME Regulations, 
2024, which were published on the NMC w ebsite on September 12, 2024. The process remains 
ongoing, with UGMEB committed to continuously improving the curriculum to ensure high -

7 
 
quality medical education and its effective implementation. The latest CBME guidelines, 
effective from the academic year 2024-25, introduce bilingual teaching, learning, and assessment 
modes. These will include languages such as Assamese, Bangla, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, 
Malayalam, Marathi, Odiya, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu, in addition to English. 
 
1.3.7 The Attitude, Ethics and Communication module (AETCOM) module introduced within the 
MBBS curriculum by UGMEB has been positively received by the Committee, and the board is 
actively overseeing its comprehensive implementation across medical colleges and institutions.  
 
1.3.8 The Ministry has reviewed the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) followed by NMC for 
framing regulations under NMC Act, 2019 and recommended the necessary changes to NMC. 
Accordingly, In the 11th meeting of the NMC, a new SOP was adopted. This SOP outli nes a 
structured process for drafting regulations, which includes consultations with stakeholders, legal 
vetting, and engagement with MoHFW the Ministry of Law & Justice to ensure thorough review 
and stability before any regulation is notified. 
 
1.3.9 Complaints received against medical college by the NMC are documented and appropriate 
action are taken during the annual renewal process for MBBS seats, with further action as 
deemed necessary. 
 
Research Support and facilities 
Recommendation 
1.4.1 The Committee recommends the NMC encourage the medical colleges to develop a 
tradition of research in the college so that upcoming MBBS students and later MD / MS students 
gain sufficient exposure in the research ambience of the institute. Furthermore, col leges should 
incentivize quality research both at the student and faculty level.  
(Para 2.25 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4.2 By its new guidelines, the undergraduate medical education board of NMC has mandated a 
basic research unit in all the medical colleges. This will encourage research. The guideline also 
supports and Integrative research unit for supporting modern science research in AYUSH related 
sciences. The Teachers Education Qualifications (TEQ) mandates research publication for 
promotions. Those who are pursuing Post -Graduate courses are also expected to do a research 
project as a thesis. Training in basic research methodology is also mandated. 
 
Faculty Development Programme 
 
 

8 
 
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee notes that faculty development is vital for ensuring that faculty members 
have the skills and knowledge they need to teach and train students effectively. The Committee 
understands that in our country, elementary, primary, and secondary scho ol teachers must 
undergo training in formal schools or colleges of education to be eligible for appointments and 
promotion. Still, there is no such requirement for selecting teachers in medical colleges in India. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends the NMC  to release the guidelines on the―Faculty 
Development Programme" without any delay. The policies should be formulated to support the 
achievement of the goal to enhance the quality and relevance of education for future healthcare 
professionals. These guidel ines should encompass critical areas such as clinical instruction, 
small group facilitation, large group presentations, feedback and assessment, personal and 
organizational growth, leadership, and scholarly activities. The strategies and formats for faculty 
development should exhibit flexibility, ensuring they are tailored to the specific healthcare 
requirements of our nation, institution, and learners. Faculty development programs (FDPs) can 
encompass a range of activities, including continuing education, on-the-job training, traditional 
classroom settings, in -person, online,or via tele/videoconferences, self -paced learning, 
mentorship, involvement in communities of practice, or a combination of these  approaches.  
(Para 3.14 of the report) 
1.5.2 Furthermore, the Committee notes that conducting faculty training through regional bodies 
and nodal centers has limited availability and capacity. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
establishing a National Institute for Training of Medical Teachers. A dedicated ins titute would 
provide year -round access to training for medical college faculty, effectively expanding the 
capacity for teacher development and establishing standardized quality benchmarks. This may 
also lead to the institutionalization of training procedures and best practices. 
 (Para 3.15 of the report) 
Action Taken

Faculty Shortage and the Issue of Ghost Faculty 
 
Recommendation 
3.5.1 The Committee feels that establishing additional medical colleges is undoubtedly a positive 
stride in addressing the chronic shortage of healthcare professionals. However, in this effort, it is 
crucial to ensure the production of genuinely qualified doctor s which is incumbent upon the 
presence of well -qualified and experienced faculty members. Teachers in medical colleges are 
the cornerstone of a robust medical education system, shaping not only the knowledge and skills 
but also the ethical foundations of f uture medical practitioners. The Committee believes that 
whether it is the expansion of medical colleges or the implementation of progressive initiatives 
like NMC's Competency -Based Medical Education (CBME) module, the efficacy of these 
reforms hinges on t he availability of a dedicated, skilled teaching force. The shortage of 
qualified teachers is a common thread in both scenarios and addressing this issue is paramount. 
In this regard, the Committee has taken note of the findings of NMC for 246 medical coll eges. 
The Committee views that NMC's efforts, like AEBAS - based attendance CCTVs in colleges, 
have yet to deliver much as issues like ghost faculty and zero faculty attendance have only 
escalated as per the NMC's assessment. Therefore, the Committee is of the consensus that the 

21 
 
faculty shortage issue in India is twofold: first, there is a genuine shortage of qualified faculty 
members, and second, even the available faculty often lacks the inclination to teach at the 
college level. To address the issue of ghost faculty and ensure that the available faculty comes to 
the college to teach, the Committee recommends the Government to strictly enforce the 
regulations already in place to curb the problem of ghost faculty and zero attendance. NMC 
should conduct regul ar inspections of medical colleges and take action against colleges that are 
found to be violating the regulations.  
(Para 3.5 of the report) 
3.5.2 Additionally, streamlining the recruitment process is imperative. The significant delays in 
the recruitment process must be reduced through the simplification of bureaucratic procedures 
and the incorporation of technology for quicker application processing and interview scheduling. 
An efficient recruitment process is necessary to expedite faculty appointments an d fill vacant 
positions without unnecessary delays. NMC should make it easier for students and parents to 
report ghost faculty and zero attendance. Furthermore, the Committee feels that the Government 
should undertake some essential steps for retaining fac ulty viz. improved working conditions for 
faculty members, transparent career progression paths, etc. Clear criteria and milestones for 
promotions by recognising and rewarding excellence in teaching, research, and clinical work 
need to be chalked out. Regu lar performance evaluations are crucial in identifying and 
addressing concerns promptly.  
(Para 3.6 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.5.3 The NMC has by its guidelines stipulated minimum standard requirements. This includes 
the minimum numbers of staff to be available for teaching the given number of MBBS students. 
There are several challenges which have led to what may appear as shortage of  faculty. As a 
consequence, ghost faculty has become a curse to medical education. Some faculty either do not 
come regularly or put false attendance. There are places where all faculty are not appointed as the 
matter may be under the state government. 
 
3.5.4 Sanctioning of posts and the reservations may also come in the way of filling all vacancies 
completely. In the most places faculty are appointed on contract or on ad -hoc basis that does not 
provide any incentive for retaining the faculty. Salary in a te acher's job may be less attractive 
compared to private practice. Colleges which are distantly located from urban areas have 
different challenges in getting faculty. Services required for the family, e.g., education of the 
children, produce another challeng e to move out to urban places for jobs. Incentivizing the post 
of a teacher can be an alternative to attract enough number of faculty. Together, there are 
multiple approaches to improve faculty presence and overcome the shortage. 
 
3.5.5 The teachers' educa tional qualifications regulation is being revised to be inclusive and 
hence augment faculty pool that can be resourced for purpose of medical education. Increased 

22 
 
availability of PG seats by doubling of the numbers in the last 10 years can also help mitiga ting 
the shortage. Still, there are some branches of medical education, particularly the lab -based 
departments, where there are different challenges. 
 
3.5.6 NMC has introduced the Adhaar based biometric attendance system that is expected to 
monitor better attendance from the appointed faculty. Improvements in this monitoring by way of 
more robust IT solutions that include face recognition, and geo positioning monitoring of 
attendance will add to the sensitivity of monitoring the faculty attendance and hence  mitigate the 
menace of ghost faculty. 
 
Further recommendation 
3.5.7 The Committee feels that to address faculty shortages in medical colleges, especially in 
remote areas, it is essential to provide incentives for teaching positions. The Committee is of 
the considered view that c ompetitive salaries, job security, and structured career growth 
need to be prioritized over ad -hoc or contractual appointments  for streamlining and 
strengthening the faculty. Such emphasis will ensure the production of generally qualified 
doctors and instituting a robust medical education system . In this regard, the Committee is 
in agreement with the  Government, however,  the Committee would further recommend  
that special incentives such as housing support, education facilities for children, and rural 
service allowance need to be introduced  to attract and retain faculty in distant locations. 
The Committee reiterates that c lear criteria and milestones for promotions by recognizing 
and rewarding excellence in teaching, research, and clinical work are required to embedded 
in the system. Regular performance evaluations are crucial in identifying well-qualified and 
experienced faculty members. Moreover, streamlining the sanctioning of posts and ensuring 
a balanced reservation policy will facilitate the timely filling up of vacancies, ultimately 
strengthening medical education and healthcare services. 
3.5.8 The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry that Ghost Faculty is undoubtedly a 
curse to the medical education,  however, Committee believes that recently introduced 
‘Aadhar based Biometric Attendance System by NMC’ regarding attendance, would go a 
long way in combating and curbing the problem of Ghost Faculty and Zero Attendance. 
Administrative monitoring by way of most robust IT solutions viz. face recognition and geo 
positioning monitoring of attendance would definitely give impetus to the sensitivity of 
monitoring the faculty attendance and hence mitigate the menace of ghost faculty.  
 
Foreign Medical Graduates 
 
Recommendation 
3.6.1 The Committee believes that the FMG Regulations 2021 are a pivotal framework to 

23 
 
maintain and uphold the quality of medical professionals in India. However, these regulations 
must adopt a facilitative role rather than imposing unwarranted obstacles in the r egistration and 
internship process for foreign medical graduates. The NMC should address the inconsistencies in 
granting permanent registration to foreign medical graduates across various States. The 
Committee recommends the NMC strike a balance between qu ality assurance and inclusivity, 
ensuring that bureaucratic or procedural impediments do not unduly burden foreign medical 
graduates who meet the necessary standards. By acting as facilitators, regulatory authorities can 
streamline the registration and int ernship procedures, enhancing the integration of foreign 
medical graduates into the Indian healthcare system.  
(Para 4.7 of the report) 
3.6.2 Alternatively, the Committee has also taken note of the fact that with the expansion of the 
number of medical colleges in India, the reliance on Foreign Medical Graduates to maintain the 
doctor to population ratio may dwindle in the near future. Moreover, the Committee has also 
come across the fact that given the high standards of medical education in India, several FMGs 
are unable to clear the examination process despite several attempts. Given the future scenario, 
the Committee recommends that the Governm ent take a serious view on this issue and come up 
with some advisories to dissuade students from pursing medical education abroad.  
(Para 4.8 of the report) 
Action Taken  
3.6.3 NMC is concerned with the high numbers of students seeking admission outside the 
country for MBBS studies. These colleges that train Indian students leading to MBBS courses are 
not under direct supervision or monitoring by the NMC. Therefore, the foreign medical graduate 
license examination was conducted and is continued to be oper ational and is a major step. Over 
and above this testing, the foreign medical graduate regulation mandates one year of compulsory 
rotating medical internship as an additional training in medical education hospitals or in big non -
teaching hospitals. The eli gibility to study such course requires the NEET passing ranks, 
eligibility, like for all other MBBS students in our country. 
 
3.6.4 To discourage such outflow of aspiring medical graduates, and facilitate their education in 
the country, the national medica l commission and its predecessor, the Medical Council of India 
(BOG) have together contributed to the medical education opportunities, MBBS seats, in the 
country. There is a scope to improve this number. If the rule of hundred MBBS seats per million 
population is put to practice, another 40,000 seats can be added in our country. This will help 
medical education for aspirants in colleges that are under supervision and monitoring of the 
National Medical Commission. 
 
Further Recommendation  
3.6.5 The Committee observes that, in view of huge number of MBBS aspiring students and 
limited MBBS seats in various colleges, high number of students seek admission outside the 

24 
 
country, however, the foreign medical graduate  have to face the herculean  challenges in 
passing license examination and seeking permanent registration across various States . The 
Foreign Medical Graduate Regulation  2021 mandates one year of compuls ory rotating 
medical internship as an additional training in medical education hospitals  or in big non -
teaching hospitals. Since, to some extent, foreign medical graduates is useful in maintaining 
the doctor to population ratio, therefore, the Committee reiterates its recommendation that 
FMG Regulations 2021 should Act as facilitator thereby streamlining the registration and 
internship procedures while keeping the quality assurance of Indian Healthcare System.  
3.6.6 The Committee also understands that  it is the responsibility of the Government of the 
day to curb the outflow of aspiring medical graduates and facilitate their education in the 
country. In order to improve the doctor to population ratio  and to reduce the reliance on  
foreign medical graduates it would be appropriate  for the Government  to encourage  
expansion of medical colleges in the country to accommodate the education of MBBS 
aspiring students in the country itself. The Committee takes note of the UG -MSR 
Guidelines 2023 that prescribes 100 MBBS seats per million population and an additional 
40000 seats, if added, will meet this ratio requirement. The Committee is of considered view 
that the Government shall make concerted efforts to implement the prescribed 100 seats 
per million population as per UG -MSR 2023 guidelines.  Moreover, the Committee also 
takes note of the Budget announcement 2025 -26 regarding the addition of 10,000 seats in 
the medical colleges during 2025 -26 and addition of 75,000 seats in next five years. The 
Committee is of the firm view that once the Budge t announcement is implemented the 
MBBS aspirant students would hardly need to move outside the country  for seeking 
medical education.  
Graduate Outcome Assessment & NMC EXIT Test 
 
Recommendation 
3.7.1 The Committee acknowledges that the NMC intends to introduce a standardized 
assessment of medical graduates through the National Exit Test (NExT). The Committee notes 
that standardized assessment of medical graduates would ensure that all medical graduate s have 
a uniform level of knowledge and skills, regardless of where they studied. This improves the 
quality of medical education and training in India and makes the process of licensure and 
postgraduate admissions more transparent and fairer. The Act provi des for three years for 
unrolling of NExT, the Committee has taken note that NExT is yet to be implemented.  
(Para 4.11 of the report) 
 
3.7.2 Given the pivotal role the NExT exam is poised to play in medical education, the 
Committee recommends the Government exhaustively examine the implications of 
implementation. The Committee advocates for meticulous due diligence in addressing the 
concerns of all relevant stakeholders. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the 

25 
 
Government allocate ample time for thorough preparation and provide an early release of the 
exam schedule, along with other relevant details regarding the examination. This will enable the 
first batch of candidates to prepare adequately and smoothly transition t o the new examination 
format. Additionally, considering the diverse background of medical colleges from which the 
first batch of NExT aspirants would come, the Committee suggests that the evaluation criteria 
should be moderate. It is imperative to ensure t hat no group of graduates faces an undue 
advantage or disadvantage in the examination. Striking a fair and equitable balance in the 
evaluation process will be pivotal in ensuring the success and fairness of the NExT exam.  
(Para 4.12 of the report) 
 
3.7.3 Moreover, the Committee believes in addition to standardised final assessment of 
graduates, there is an urgent need to universalize or standardise undergraduate and postgraduate 
education. Reputed institutes like AIIMS impart different quality of medica l education while 
newly opened medical institutes need such quality. Keeping this in view, the Committee 
recommends the Government to divide India into zones, and in each zone reputed institutes like 
AIIMS can function as mentor institutes for all the othe r medical colleges in that zone. Mentor 
institutes shall play a significant role in monitoring the standard of education and the classes in 
the newly set medical colleges or private medical colleges.  
(Para 4.13 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
3.7.4 Introduction of NEXT marks a substantial shift in MBBS education. Its examination format 
differs significantly from NEET. The implementation of NEXT is set to bring significant changes 
to university examinations as well. It has the potential to impact teac hing methods, learning 
approaches, and other assessments throughout MBBS courses, starting from the earliest stages. 
Additionally, the simultaneous introduction of a Post -internship Practical Examination at the end 
of the internship period is also a new development. 
 
3.7.5 The regulations for the National Exit Test (NEXT) were published by NMC 28.06.2023 
however considering the response, the Government under NMC Act, 2019 defer the 
implementation and decided to examine the matter relating to implementation/ preparation of 
conducting the NExT exam. Accordingly, the Ministry appointed a Committee on 03.10.2023 
headed by DGHS for recommendation to implement NEXT -1. Subsequently, the committee was 
reconstituted under the Chairmanship of Member, NITI Aayog to take  this matter forward. 
Meetings of the Committee have been convened for decided way forward. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.7.6 The Committee is of the considered view that introduction of NExT will instill a 
universal  and standardized assessment of medical graduates having uniform level of 

26 
 
knowledge and skills and ultimately leading to quality medical education and training 
across the country. The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry that NExT indicate a 
paradigm shift in teaching methods, learning approaches, critical assessment through 
MBBS courses. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Committee reconstituted 
under the Chairmanship of Members, NITI Aayog would submit its recommendation at the 
first opportunity for implementation of NExT Exam as per pre -conceived schedule. The 
Committee is also in agreement with the Ministry that the simultaneous introduction of a 
Post-internship Practical Examination at the end of the internship period would further 
ensure fair and equitable balance in the process of license, evaluation process and post -
graduate admission.  
 
3.7.7 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that th e Government should divide 
India into different zones and in each zone reputed institutes like AIIMS can function as 
mentor institutes for all the other medical colleges in that zone. Mentor institutes shall play 
a significant role in monitoring the standa rd of education and the classes in the newly set 
medical colleges or private medical colleges.

Affordability of Medical Education 
Recommendation 
4.1.1 The Committee further recommends the Ministry to formulate a comprehensive framework 
to address bureaucratic hurdles and effectively implement the partnership of private medical 
colleges with the district hospitals. The Committee belie ves that this initiative will not only

functioning cost of private colleges, thereby rationalizing the costs of medical education.

setting up of―Skill Labs in private colleges as they are sophisticated and costly and are often

economically disadvantaged students in covering their tuition fees. These scholarships could be

medical education for all.  
(Para 2.30 of the report) 
Action  Taken

difficulties.

1. The Committee appreciates that the World Federation of Medical Education

role for c onsolidating high quality medical education in the country which is in fact, the 
basic foundation upon which the competent and compassionate healthcare 
professionals/system are superimposed. NMC is required to ensure quality medical 
education for fostering  affordability, accessibility, and availability of next generations 
healthcare needs. The Committee is of the considered view that only robust & modern 
medical education system with adequate investment on advanced physical infrastructure

quality education system across the country with due impetus on evidence base d practices

ethical integrity and social behavioral inclination amongst medical practitioners.

 2. The Committee notes with concern the fact that there is uneven distribution of 
medical seats across the country as some States have a high concentration of medical seats

Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the NMC must come forward with

(Para 3.2.3)

1.1. The Committee takes into account the thematic areas of Ayush activities and the institutional 
framework to achieve the objectives of those activities. The Committee desires that each and 
every institution must strive towards achievin g the Mission Objective of the Ministry of Ayush 
within the specified time framework. The Committee further observes that the broad thematic 
area of Ayush activities is the key to accomplish the mission objectives of the Ministry i.e., 
improve access to hi gh quality and affordable Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Sowa -Rigpa 
(AUS&SR) & Homeopathy medical education, availability of adequate and high quality 
AUS&SR & Homeopathy medical professionals in all parts of the country, promote equitable and 
universal healt hcare that encourages community health perspective. The thematic area of

CCRAS, CCRUM, CCRS, CCRH and CCRYN. The Committee, however, feels that in order to 
address emerging challenges of healthcare, there is a need for functional integration of Ayurveda 
and conventional medicine with its affordable and evidence based use to boost Ayurveda in the 
paradigm of contemporary scientific, technological and medical parameters.

● Ministry of Ayush issued an advisory in accordance with letter no. K -11023/01/2012-
DCC (Ayush) dated December 8, 2023, which clarifies that the permissible limits of 
heavy metals do not apply to Ayurvedic, Siddha, or Unani formulations where such 
metals are utilized as ingredients or in the processing of the formulation. This advisory i s 
pertinent and clarifies the regulatory framework in accordance with Section 3(a) of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.  
As prescribed in Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereunder, enforcement of the 
legal provisions pertaining to Quality Co ntrol and issuance of drug license of Ayurveda, Siddha, 
Unani and Homoeopathy drugs, is vested with the State Drug Controllers/ State Licensing 
Authorities appointed by the concerned State/ Union Territory Government. Rule 158 -B in the 
Drugs Rules, 1945 pr ovides the regulatory guidelines for issue of license to manufacture 
Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani medicines and Rule 85 (A to I) in the Drugs Rules, 1945 provides the 
regulatory guidelines for issue of license to manufacture Homoeopathy medicines. It is 
mandatory for the manufacturers to adhere to the prescribed requirements for licensing of 
manufacturing units & medicines including proof of safety & effectiveness, compliance with the 
Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) as per Schedule T & Schedule M -I for Ayurveda, Siddha, 
Unani drugs and Homoeopathy drugs respectively of the Drugs Rules, 1945 and quality standards 
of drugs given in the respective pharmacopoeia.  
Moreover, Drug Inspectors collect medicine samples regularly from manufacturing firms or sale 
shops with in their jurisdiction and sent it to Drug Testing Laboratory under Drug Control 
department for quality testing and if any sample found to be Not of Standard Quality, appropriate 
action initiates such as preventing the sale of the products from the mar ket and appropriate legal 
actions as per Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules made thereunder.

3.28 The Committee understands that Utilization Certificate (UC) in government systems is a

spent. Moreover, UC ensures transparency and accountability by demonstrating that the fund 
allocation has been used for its intended purpose and not misappropriated, and that the project 
achieved its desired outcomes. In this light the Committee has observed and recommended time 
and again regarding the delay in clearing pending UCs. The Committee expresses concern over 
pending UCs to number of 1549 involving Rs. 1608.29 during 2023 -24 and a total  number of 
1521 pending UCs involving an amount to the tune of Rs. 1765.85 in 2024 -25. The Committee 
observes that the largest share in pending UCs is that of NAM with 897 UCs worth Rs 1592.09 
crores. Timely submission of UCs is very crucial in scheme moni toring, subsequent release of 
funds and successful implementation of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends that the Ministry must expedite its efforts in liquidating UCs as per standard 
timeline set for the activity. States/UTs may be p ersuaded and encouraged to use the NAM portal 
efficiently for the submitting UCs, SAAPs etc. 
(Para 4.2.2 ibid)

expedited, particularly focusing on the clinical validation of AYUSH practices. Enhanced 
inter-departmental coordination is crucial for integrating AYUSH into broader national 
health strategies and fostering international collaboration. 
(Para 3.39.2 of the ATR) 
40. The Committee acknowledges and appreciates the commendable efforts of AIIA and 
CCRAS in advancing AYUSH through clinical services, international collaborations, 
research initiatives, capacity building, and public health programs. However, considering 
the Ministry of AYUSH encompasses multiple institutions and autonomous bodies, the 
Committee seeks clarification on whether the onus of these initiatives will rest exclusively 
with AIIA and CCRAS. Additionally, while the Ministry has articulated an ambition to 
realize a market capitalization of USD 200 billion for AYUSH within next five year s, the 
Committee urges the submission of a detailed, year -wise strategic plan outlining 
implementation frameworks, institutional responsibilities, and resource allocation. A 
comprehensive response with details of schemes and plans for growth and developmen t of 
Ayush activities and the Ministry should project a much more enhanced budgetary 
allocation. 
(Para 3.40.2 of the ATR) 
 

150 
 
41. The Committee appreciates the bilateral agreement of the Ministry of Ayush with 
the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to include Ayush products. The Committee 
however wants to know the steps taken by the Ministry of Ayush to establish Ayush specific 
healthcare centres in PHCs/CHCs at district level in all the states across India. The 
Committee appreciates the larger goal of the Mini stry of Ayush to have 30 lakh ayush 
professionals in the country by 2047. However, to effectively realize the goal it is imperative 
on the part of the Ministry to split it into short term goals. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Ayu sh come up with comprehensive yearly plans of 
producing a minimum number of say 1 lakh Ayush Professionals each year. In extension, 
the Ministry must chalk out the plan for absorption of these professionals in appropriate 
jobs. Hence job creation is a must  in Ayush Healthcare to achieve the cherished goals of 
Ayush@2047. Further, as suggested by NISR, the Committee endorses the opinion that to 
provide health to all it is suggested to strengthen the local health traditions and train the 
traditional healer in primary health care in remote areas. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry of Ayush to find out the traditional health practitioners in remotest areas of the 
country and archive their knowledge in traditional healing which can be utilized for a 
larger population of this country and beyond.  
(Para 3.41.2 of the ATR) 
42. The Committee observes that the Ministry of AYUSH has undertaken commendable 
initiatives to promote AYUSH systems globally, notably through the International 
Cooperation Scheme, academic col laborations, and the implementation of accredited 
training programs under the Ayurveda Training Accreditation Board (ATAB) and Yoga 
Certification Board (YCB). The contributions of institutions such as AIIA, CCRAS and 
ITRA in disseminating and operationaliz ing these programs are noteworthy. However, the 
action taken does not fully align with the Committee‟s recommendation in letter and spirit 
to significantly enhance global participation in Yoga and Ayurveda training. However, the 
current measures appear to remain largely domestic in scope and lack a comprehensive 
international outreach framework. The Committee strongly feels that there is an immense 
potential in Ayush systems on the global stage and it must be promoted on a global level 
based on unique stren gths of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Rigpa -
Sowa and Homeopathy. It is recommended that the Ministry develop a cohesive global 
strategy encompassing international partnerships, welcoming international students to get 
Yoga Certification in India under aforementioned schemes. The Ministry of Ayush should 
strive to make the ayurveda institutes of highest international repute, that all over the 
world people would want to get education in traditional system of medicine especially in 
Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy to begin with.  
(Para 3.42.2 of the ATR)

CHAPTER- I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1 Mandate of DHR 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee takes note of the allocation of a new Business to DHR in the form of 
Health Technology Assessment which will promote evidence -based decision making across the 
healthcare spectrum. An allocation of business suggests enhanced responsibility for managing the 
specific allocation, impacting its policy formulation, its implementation as well as coordination 
with other ministries. This also translates into additional financial implications like need for 
increased budgetary allocation to cover the new responsibilities, including staff recruitment, 
infrastructure development, etc. Accordingly, it is expected that DHR takes appropriate measures 
to continue to execute this crucial role and is also able to secure and utilise adequate allocation of 
funds for the work. 
(Para 1.2.3 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 Department of Health Research (DHR) has been taking appropriate steps to enhance the 
funds for HTA. The BE for the attached office for year 2024 -25 was 10 crores and RE was 
enhanced to 17.80 Crores. The BE allocation for year 2025-26 is 18.75 Crores. 
1.2 Human Resource Management 
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee, even though aware of the funding limitations, is not fully convinced of 
the adequateness of a consolidated stipend of Rs.1.2 lakhs per month for 3 years for a selected 
researcher under the Scheme to attract professionals from abroad. The Com mittee feels that the 
Department should consider keeping the window open to enhance the quantum of stipend, at 
least based on the project proposals presented and the remuneration the person is receiving in the 
foreign country. The same flexible approach sh ould be adopted in case of the quantum of grant, 
the Committee desires.  Accordingly, to address the intricate issue of brain drain, India must 
adopt a comprehensive strategy that includes enhancing higher education, strengthening research 
infrastructure, and implementing policies to improve the standard of living. These measures 
would encourage skilled Indian professionals to return from abroad and undertake domestic 
health research projects.  A unified and long -term approach is essential for India to reta in and 
recover its most valuable asset—human capital. 
(Para 1.3.7 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 Under HRD scheme component of NRI/PIO/OCI Research Support, in addition to the 
stipend, research grants of upto Rs 20 lacs/year for a maximum of 5 years are also provided to the 

2 
 
Fellows. Government has been able to successfully align the output of the scheme with the goal 
of attracting and retaining the diaspora researchers within India.  There have been some fellows 
of the scheme who have taken up regular positions in academic and research institutions in India. 
1.2.3 Apart from the Department of Health Research Initiative for encouraging the Indian 
diaspora to engage in research, VAIBHAV Fellowship is being implemented by th e DST. The 
VAIBHAV Fellowship aims at improving the research ecosystem of India‘s Higher Education 
and Scientific Institutions by facilitating academic and research collaborations between Indian 
Institutions and the best institutions in the world through m obility of faculty/researchers from 
overseas institutions to India. 
Key Features of the VAIBHAV Fellowship Programme: 
● Knowledge Verticals: The programme focuses on 18 identified knowledge verticals, 
including quantum technology, health, pharmaceuticals, el ectronics, agriculture, energy, 
computer sciences, and material sciences, among others. 
● Eligibility: The fellowship is open to outstanding scientists and technologists of Indian 
origin (NRI)/ (PIO)/ (OCI) who are actively engaged in research activities in their 
respective countries. 
● Collaboration Duration: Selected fellows will have the opportunity to work in 
collaboration with Indian Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs),  universities, and 
public-funded scientific institutions. 
● They may spend up to two mo nths per year, for a maximum of three years, at an Indian 
institution of their choice. 
1.2.4 The Hon‘ble Committee suggestions on enhancing higher education, strengthening 
research infrastructure and implementing policies to improve the standing of living of researchers 
have been taken due cognizance. DHR has already started working towards these through its 
various measures,  some of which are as follows: 1) To increase the pool of trained medical 
researchers, a Young Medical Faculty -PhD Support programme h as been started by DHR since 
2024. Recently, Expressions of Interest were invited from Institutes of National Importance 
(INIs), having their own MD -PhD or post MD-PhD degree program and who are willing to come 
on board this Medical PhD program, so that th e fellowships can be supported for the integrated 
Medical PhD programme.  2) A liberal equipment and consumables grant is provided in HRD 
scheme to strengthen research infrastructure. 3) DHR has also been implementing different 
schemes like MRU/MRHRU, PM -ABHIM, VRDL, etc towards strengthening of research 
infrastructure, their outlays have been improved in recent years. 4) The stipend amounts of 
JRF/SRF have been revised and increased in 2024 and the House Rent Allowance (HRA) Support 
component has also been added to women and young scientists in HRD scheme. 
 
 

3 
 
 
Recommendation 
1.2.5 Further, the Department should look into the possibility of involving private sector which 
can contribute through competitive pay packages, which would be well within t heir realm as 
promotion of PPP. 
(Para 1.3.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2.6 As part of this effort, DHR is in the process of establishing the Medical Innovation 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC): a special purpose vehicle envisioned as a strategic 
institutional mechanism to drive biomedical innov ation through effective public -private 
collaboration. Through this proposed section 8 company, we plan to engage Indian talent in 
Health Research in the private sector in contributing to the national health priorities of India.   
1.3 Landmarks in Health Research in India 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 While going through the major landmarks in Health Research in India in the last decade, 
the Committee notices that the India has done considerably well in the field of Communicable 
Diseases, commensurate to its own needs as well as to contributing the global knowledge pool. 
The Committee is appreciative of this achievement. The India Disease Burden Study, mentioned 
by the Department as a breakthrough initiative, provided  crucial insights into the shifting burden 
of diseases in India, highlighting the growing prevalence of Non -Communicable diseases 
(NCDs). Going by the indicators provided by the Study, India‘s efforts in the area of NCDs needs 
further impetus. 
(Para 1.4.1of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 ICMR research in NCD continued to expand and strengthen its diverse portfolio, 
addressing critical and contemporary health challenges. The primary focus remains on the 
prevention, diagnosis, and management of chronic condi tions, including Oncology, 
Cardiovascular Diseases, Mental Health, Neurological Sciences, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolic 
Syndrome, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases, Gastroenterology, Geriatrics, Oral Health, 
Orthopedics, and Nephrology & Urology, wi th efforts directed toward the prevention, diagnosis, 
and management of chronic health conditions. 
1.3.3 Additionally, research activities have continued in the fields of Otorhinolaryngology , 
Hematology, Anesthesiology, and Disability, Rehabilitation, and Assistive Technology. Other 
key areas of focus included Trauma, Accidents and Injuries, Environmental and Occupational 
Health, Climate Change, Tobacco, and Chronic Disease Health Research. M ultidisciplinary 

4 
 
studies in Toxicology, Anatomy, Anthropology, Nanomedicine, and Traditional Medicine also 
highlighted ICMR‘ commitment to advancing innovation in healthcare and biomedicalsciences. 
1.3.4 Some of the achievements i.e. Initiatives of the Nat ional importance of the past year may 
be highlighted as: 
(i) Cancer care: 
a.  CARE-Clinical Pharmacology –ICMR‘s CARE- Clinical Pharmacology initiative 
focused on therapeutic monitoring of anti -cancer drugs such as sunitinib and 
docetaxel, showing that dru g monitoring improved patients‘ quality of life (QOL) 
and reduced treatment costs.  
b.  PFOS (PREVALL): ICMR, in collaboration with Tata Memorial Center -
ACTREC, developed a powder for oral suspension (PFOS) of 6 -mercaptopurine 
(PREVALL), which helps in acc urate dosing for children undergoing treatment 
for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL). Since children aged 1 –10 often face 
difficulties swallowing tablets, this liquid formulation of 6 -MP helps in 
overcoming this issue and ensures better treatment outcome s. The product, 
expected to benefit approximately 10,000 children annually, was patented and 
launched on November 25, 2023. 
(ii) Cardiovascular Disease 
a. PACT-HF Trial – This trial, aimed at preventing repeat hospital admissions and 
death in Heart Failure patients, recruited 1,693 patients, with a 97% follow-up rate 
and a 9% mortality rate at six months. 
b. The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) – IHCI has successfully 
expanded to 154 districts, enrolling over 5.1 million hypertensive patients ac ross 
22,000 health facilities, including 16,000 Health & Wellness Centers. Nearly half 
(47%) of the registered patients have achieved BP control. 
c. STEMI Care Pathway: Implemented in districts of Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, 
Uttar Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh,  this initiative demonstrated that STEMI 
patients can be diagnosed at CHC level via tele -ECG and  receive life saving 
thrombolytic therapy. The model has since been upscaled to the entire state of 
Himachal Pradesh, Punjab and 4 districts of Andhra Pradesh. 
(iii) Stroke and Neurological Research 
a. INSTRuCT Clinical Trials – The Indian Stroke Clinical Trial Network 
(INSTRuCT) was established to create a cutting -edge stroke clinical trial 
infrastructure in India. Initially, INSTRuCT Phase I undertook two clini cal 
trials across 30 centers. The network expanded in Phase II, encompassing 

5 
 
58 centers. Currently, four clinical trials are ongoing under this network, 
each addressing distinct aspects of stroke care and treatment. 
b. FeSSH Trial – (Fever, hyperglycemia, swallowing and hypertension  
management in acute stroke: Stepped wedged cluster randomized trial with 
cross-sectional data collection): Baseline data were collected across 20 
centers, with 12 centers transitioning to the intervention phase. A total of 
3,022 eligible patients were identified from a screened population of 4,818. 
c. SMRUTHI India – The Strategic Multimodal Intervention in At -Risk 
Elderly Indians for the Prevention of Dementia (SMRUTHI India) aims to 
establish a prospective longitudinal cohort o f elderly individuals with 
multiple risk factors (CAIDE ≥ 6) and develop a validated multimodal ―care 
bundle‖ intervention in four MRHRU field areas. 
(iv) Diabetes Research 
a. Indian Diabetic Risk Score: The Indian Diabetic Risk Score was evaluated 
and found to be a cost-effective tool for screening diabetes in Asian Indians. 
b. INDIAB Study: The INDIAB study provided state -specific obesity 
prevalence data for better policy planning of the nationalprogram and 
suggested age -specific HbA1c cut -offs to minimiz e over -diagnosis of 
diabetes, especially in elderly individuals. The survey was completed in 30 
states/ UTs, with follow -up studies completed in  Arunachal Pradesh and 
Tamil Nadu and the data is being analyzed. The study in the Union 
Territories has also been completed. 
c. Dietary Recommendations: ICMR‘s research also highlighted the 
importance of dietary changes for diabetes management. The data 
recommended reducing carbohydrates and increasing protein intake for 
Type 2 diabetes (T2D) remission and preventi ng progression from pre -
diabetes to T2D. 
d. Young Diabetes Registry: ICMR‘s Young Diabetes Registry reported 
critical data on the prevalence of Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, along with 
complications such as retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy. This 
registry also documented a high incidence of co -morbidities such as 
autoimmune thyroid disease and hypertension in diabetic patients. 
Recommendation 
1.3.5 Accordingly, the Committee observes that the policies, priorities and funding for health 
research in the country should be optimally aligned with its actual health needs rather than with 
the global research agenda. Hence, India should prioritise research o n under-studied diseases in 

6 
 
the country, such as cardiovascular, respiratory diseases, etc. along with research on public 
health, healthcare infrastructure/systems and implementation of clinical medicine. The 
Committee feels that alignment of health resear ch with the National Health Policy & Priorities 
would be cardinal in this direction and hence recommends, accordingly. 
(Para 1.4.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.3.6 In addition to Extramural and Intramural projects, a separate program has been 
established to fund projects addressing National Health Research Priorities, which are directly 
monitored by the Director General (DG) of ICMR. These priorities with relevant re search 
questions, identified by the Scientific Advisory Board (SAB) and approved by the Governing 
Council (GC), are determined based on feedback from multiple stakeholders. National Health 
Research Programme (NHRP) is being implemented as a mission -mode initiative with directed 
research efforts toward 12 areas of pressing national importance. 
1.3.7 In June 2023, total 16 projects were decided under areas of communicable diseases – TB, 
Vector Borne Diseases, and Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR); under non -communicable diseases 
– Cancer, Mental Health, and Ambulatory Care; under reproductive, child health, and nutrition – 
Anemia, Childhood Malnutrition, and Neonatal Mortality; and other areas such as Acute 
Emergency Care and Oral Health. NHRP proposals came into mission mode and funding initiated 
for proposals in 2024. Additionally, Primary Health Care was included in this list based on a 
request from NITI Aayog, recognizing its importance in delivering care for all these conditions. 
The duration of these projects  will be a maximum of four years, extendable by one year with the 
approval of the competent authority. As of date 30 NHRP projects in different health research 
priorities are being carried out. 
1.4 Role of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in Health Research Funding 
Recommendation 
1.4.1 The Committee reckons that since the Government is always under compulsion to 
apportion the limited financial resources amongst the varied needs of the country, it would be 
prudent to leverage the financial resources, technological expertise and innovation  capabilities of 
the Private sector in furthering the needs of the health sector, especially in research. The 
Committee holds the view that when 102 cutting edge research and innovation outcomes, 
produced in collaboration with the Private sector, are dovet ailed with policy initiatives and wide 
access infrastructure of the Government, it can change the health care landscape of India. Taking 
into account the fact that promotion of public -private partnership is one of the businesses 
allocated to DHR as per the  Allocation of Business Rules of the Government of India. The

1.5 Emerging Technologies and Ethical Concerns related to Health Research  
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee recognises the importance of adoption of new technologies, innovation 
and constant endeavour for development of new drugs and treatment methods. Clinical trials are 
an inalienable data generating component of this continuing quest. The regulatory architecture 
now in place in the Country are taken note of, however, the Committee would like to emph asise 
the need to ensure ‗informed‘ consent of the participants of clinical trials which should invariably 
include sharing of information beforehand about how the data generated out of the trial would be 
used or shared. It is important to ensure that the p articipants fully understand the risks and 
benefits of a study, management of sensitive personal information and balancing the need for 
research advancement with individual privacy rights. Digitalization and sharing of patient 
information bears privacy imp lications that needs to be addressed and fixed with appropriate 
provisions. 
(Para 1.6.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.5.2 ICMR emphasizes the primacy of informed consent, underscoring that the rights, safety, 
and well-being of research participants must remain the highest priority. This principle is clearly 
articulated in the National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Hea lth Research involving 
Human Participants, 2017 published by ICMR. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) 
rules, 2019 also gives a format of preparing informed consent documents. In case of clinical 
trials, ethics approval is provided only after scrutinizing the informed consent documents; both in 
English and the relevant regional language. Funds released by ICMR for the research project are 
conditional to the valid ethics approval documents.  
1.5.3 In alignment with these guidelines, it is standard resea rch practice that the Principal 
Investigator (PI) and the designated study staff responsible for obtaining informed consent are 
adequately trained prior to the initiation of any study. Patient information sheets are prepared in 
languages that are comprehen sible to potential participants and they are given ample 
opportunities to clarify the doubts, if any. The patient information sheet clearly describes the 
risks and benefits of participating in the study, the voluntariness of participation and that there 
will be no negative impact of non-participation or withdrawal from the trial.   
1.5.4 It is ensured that all the clinical trials that are conducted and coordinated by ICMR follow 
the principles of ethics and written informed consent is appropriately obtained . It is also ensured 
that confidentiality of data is maintained by the study team. Data collected digitally is always 
anonymized and personal identifiers such as name are not collected.

1.24 Public-Private partnerships in medical research  
Recommendation 
1.24.1 The Committee observes the move of DHR -ICMR to set up a Section 8 Company, 
MIDAC, to foster innovation in medical field by handholding healthcare innovators. This move 
would help them to overcome the challenges of developmental stages and get their 
technology/product to the market. The Committee feels that along with promoting scientific 
talent, it is equally important to create avenues for the researchers and innovators to market their 
products/findings. Regulatory frameworks, a technology/product has to g o through during 
developmental stages, has been put in place to ensure the quality, safety and effectiveness of the 
product. However, many a times, innovators find traversing this labyrinth more difficult than 
discovering the product itself. Hence, it is o nly appropriate that the developmental stages, a new 

30 
 
technology/product has to go through, before it can be commercially made available, are 
christened as ‗Valley of Death‖.  
(Para 4.13.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.24.2  In response to the Hon‘ble  Committee's recommendations, the Department of Health 
Research has envisioned several focused interventions under MIDAC, including the MedTech 
Mitra initiative, to directly address the challenges faced by healthcare innovators: 
i)   Establishment of MIDAC as a Section 8 Company: MIDAC is proposed to be 
established as a not -for-profit corporate entity under the Companies Act, 2013, 
with the core mandate to facilitate the translation of research into commercially 
viable products. MIDAC will act as a central platform to address barriers in 
clinical validation, intellectual property management, regulatory navigation and 
technology transfer. 
ii)  Bridging the "Valley of Death": Recognizing the developmental void many 
innovations face, MIDAC will provide structur ed handholding, grant support and 
validation infrastructure. Through dedicated sub -schemes like Validation and 
Evaluation Support to Medical Innovations (VESMI)  and Biomedical Product 
Development and Management (BPDM) , MIDAC will fund innovations from 
early-stage concept through to regulatory-ready status. 
iii) MedTech Mitra Platform Operationalization: Under MIDAC, the MedTech Mitra 
platform will be scaled up to assist startups, SMEs and academic innovators by 
providing expert guidance on regulatory pathwa ys, clinical trials and IP filing. It 
will facilitate access to ICMR‘s trial networks and regulatory support from 
CDSCO and engages in capacity building to empower innovators in navigating 
technical and legal requirements. 
iv) Support for Regulatory Compli ance and Risk De -Risking: MIDAC enables 
accelerated clinical validation and performance evaluation, especially for 
diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines, which often stagnate due to lack of 
regulatory clarity or infrastructural support. The platform will also assist in pre -
submission regulatory guidance and post -market surveillance studies, enhancing 
trust and product quality. 
v) Enhancing Public -Private Partnerships: MIDAC has formalized collaborations 
with industry and research organizations to promote t ranslational research through 
Public-Private Partnerships (PPP), a key mechanism to bridge resource and 
expertise gaps. 

31 
 
1.24.3  The establishment of MIDAC and the expansion of MedTech Mitra will represent a direct 
and comprehensive response to the Committee's observations. These initiatives are strategically 
designed to de -risk innovation, overcome regulatory hurdles and enable faster access of 
indigenous medical technologies to the market; thereby transforming the ―Valley of Death‖ into a 
bridge to success for Indian healthcare innovators. 
Recommendation 
1.24.4  The Committee endorses the importance of setting up a dedicated entity to handhold the 
healthcare innovators in their research to market journey. The choice of a Section 8 company also 
prima facie looks apt to the Committee as the elimination of profit motive helps in concentrating 
on the goals effectively, though there are other statutory benefits as well. The Committee desires 
the DHR to furnish the details of the rationale for setting up of MIDAC as a Section 8 Company. 
(Para 4.13.3 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.24.5 In alignment with the Hon‘ble  Committee's endorsement, the Department of Health 
Research (DHR) has strategically proposed establishment of the Medical Innovations 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC) as a Section 8 Company under the Companies Act, 
2013, for the following key reasons: 
a) Non-Profit Mandate Aligned with Public Health Goals: MIDAC is envisioned not 
as a revenue -generating enterprise but as a mission -driven enabler to bridge the 
gap between biomedical research and public access to affordable technologies. A 
Section 8 structure ensures legal and institutional alignment with public health 
imperatives, free from commercial pressures, thus maintaining scientific integrity, 
equity and transparency. 
b) Flexibility and Operational Autonomy:  As a Section 8 Company, MIDAC can 
function with greater agility and efficiency than traditional government 
departments, allowing quick decision -making in areas such as IP licensing, 
contract execution, hiring technical experts and fund mobilization. It offers a 
suitable legal platform to form multi-sectoral partnerships with academia, industry 
and international donors; critical for translational research. 
c) Statutory and Financial Advantages: MIDAC can receive grants, donations, CSR 
funds and equity -free investments and is eligible for tax exemptions under 
Sections 12AA and 80G of the Income Tax Act. These benefits make MIDAC an 
attractive and credible partner for private stakeholders and philanthropic 
institutions seeking to invest in public health innovation. 

32 
 
d) Precedents from Other Strat egic Government Initiatives: Successful Section 8 
entities such as BIRAC (DBT), iDEX (Defence)and IN -SPACe (ISRO) 
demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in driving sectoral innovation.MIDAC 
draws inspiration from these to address the unique challenges of India‘s healthcare 
innovation ecosystem; particularly for technologies with limited immediate 
commercial demand but high national health value. 
e) Institutional Synergy and IP Stewardship:  Operating under the aegis of DHR, 
MIDAC complements ICMR‘s rese arch mandate by facilitating clinical 
validation, IP protection and technology transfer —functions which require an 
independent but closely aligned organizational entity.It allows the management of 
IP rights, royalties and industry licensing with profession al autonomy, enabling 
reinvestment into innovation and ecosystem development. 
f) Accountability and Governance: MIDAC will be governed by a Board of 
Directors, including senior officials from DHR, MoHFW and independent experts, 
ensuring transparency, accountability and strategic alignment with national health 
priorities. 
1.24.6 Establishing MIDAC as a Section 8 Company allows the Department of Health Research 
to institutionalize a mission -oriented, flexible and collaborative platform dedicated to advancing 
health innovations. This model ensures the focus remains on public good rather than profit, 
aligning perfectly with the goals endorsed by the Committee and ensuring effective 
implementation of India‘s biomedical innovation strategy.
